ai-fluency-1.question: What is the primary focus of the 'AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations' course?
options: Developing meaningful and lasting human-AI collaboration skills rather than just learning temporary tech tips
Only learning how to program neural networks from scratch
Only memorizing a list of terminal commands
Completely replacing humans with machines
ai-fluency-1.explanation: The course focuses on human-AI collaboration and building lasting skills as AI technology continues to evolve.

ai-fluency-2.question: According to the course definition, 'AI Fluency' means the ability to interact with AI systems according to which 4 criteria?
options: Effective, Efficient, Ethical, and Safe
Fast, Free, Fun, and Fancy
Secret, Complex, Automatic, and Rigid
Offline, Manual, Static, and Closed
ai-fluency-2.explanation: AI Fluency = interacting with AI systems in a way that is Effective, Efficient, Ethical, and Safe.

ai-fluency-3.question: Which 4 Ds make up the core '4D Framework'?
options: Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence
Design, Develop, Deploy, and Debug
Data, Database, Docker, and Domain
Download, Delete, Duplicate, and Distribute
ai-fluency-3.explanation: The 4D Framework by Dakan, Feller, and Anthropic consists of: Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence.

ai-fluency-4.question: What is the nature of the 4 competencies (4Ds) in the AI Fluency Framework?
options: They are 4 interconnected competencies encompassing skills, knowledge, understanding, and values
They are 4 isolated steps used only once and then discarded
They are 4 names of different language models
They are 4 types of software licenses
ai-fluency-4.explanation: Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence are interconnected competencies that complement one another.

ai-fluency-5.question: What are the Three Modes of AI Interaction introduced in Chapter 1?
options: Automation, Augmentation, and Agency
Input, Process, and Output
Training, Testing, and Serving
Read, Write, and Execute
ai-fluency-5.explanation: The three ways humans collaborate with AI are Automation, Augmentation, and Agency.

ai-fluency-6.question: How is the 'Automation' interaction mode defined in AI Fluency?
options: AI completes specific tasks based on your instructions
Humans and AI brainstorm together as equal partners
AI sets its own life goals without needing humans
Humans do everything themselves without using AI
ai-fluency-6.explanation: Automation: you assign a specific task and provide clear instructions for the AI to execute that task.

ai-fluency-7.question: What does the 'Augmentation' interaction mode mean?
options: You and AI collaborate as creative thinking and task execution partners
AI runs silently in the background and never asks for your input
You only use AI for a final spell-check
AI completely replaces your decision-making authority
ai-fluency-7.explanation: Augmentation is back-and-forth interactive collaboration between humans and AI as 'thinking partners'.

ai-fluency-8.question: How does the 'Agency' interaction mode differ from 'Automation'?
options: In Agency mode, you configure AI to work independently on your behalf—establishing knowledge and behavior patterns rather than only assigning individual tasks
Agency is only used for writing short emails
Automation does not require any instructions from the user
Agency does not allow using any tools
ai-fluency-8.explanation: Agency means configuring AI to operate autonomously on your behalf based on established knowledge and behavioral rules.

ai-fluency-9.question: In the 4D Framework, what does the 'Delegation' competency mean?
options: Setting goals and deciding whether, when, and how to engage with AI
Grading the accuracy of AI outputs
Reporting to your manager that you used AI
Writing a very long prompt so the AI has to guess your intent
ai-fluency-9.explanation: Delegation is the decision-making step of dividing work: what humans do, what AI does, and what is done together.

ai-fluency-10.question: In the 4D Framework, what does the 'Description' competency focus on?
options: Effectively describing goals to prompt useful AI behaviors and outputs
Checking whether the AI has fabricated statistics
Apologizing to customers when the AI makes a mistake
Installing server hardware
ai-fluency-10.explanation: Description is the ability to communicate clearly with AI to create an effective collaborative environment.

ai-fluency-11.question: In the 4D Framework, what is the 'Discernment' competency?
options: Accurately assessing the usefulness and quality of AI outputs and behaviors
Handing over all work to AI to run automatically
Copying AI answers verbatim without reading them
Creating a free account on Claude
ai-fluency-11.explanation: Discernment helps you critically evaluate the results, process, and interaction style of AI.

ai-fluency-12.question: In the 4D Framework, what does the 'Diligence' competency emphasize?
options: Taking responsibility for what we do with AI and how we do it
Forcing AI to reply within 1 second
Using AI only to write Python code
Never letting anyone know you used AI
ai-fluency-12.explanation: Diligence ensures ethics, transparency, and safety when using and sharing AI-assisted work.

ai-fluency-13.question: What is required to practice the exercises in the AI Fluency course?
options: Only access to a large language model (such as a free Claude account or any AI chatbot)—no paid plan required
Mandatory purchase of the most expensive paid tier and a dedicated GPU
Proficiency in C++ programming
Installing Linux from source code
ai-fluency-13.explanation: The course uses Claude as an illustrative example (which has a free tier), though the principles apply to any AI system.

ai-fluency-14.question: Why does the course emphasize building 'lasting skills'?
options: Because AI technology and models change constantly, so the 4D mindset remains valuable even as new AI tools emerge
Because AI models will never be upgraded again
Because you only need to learn one single prompt trick for life
Because AI cannot learn new skills
ai-fluency-14.explanation: Model-specific tricks quickly become outdated, whereas Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence thinking retains long-term value.

ai-fluency-15.question: According to Lesson 1 Key Takeaways, effective AI collaboration requires a combination of which two elements?
options: Both practical skills and a fundamental shift in how we think about working with AI
Only fast typing speed and a strong Internet connection
Only knowing technical mathematical English
Only using a single fixed prompt
ai-fluency-15.explanation: AI Fluency requires both practical skills and a mindset that treats AI as a responsible collaborative partner.

ai-fluency-16.question: In the exercise applying the 4D Framework to a communication project, asking 'Which parts does AI do well, and which parts need a human voice?' belongs to which D?
options: Delegation
Description
Discernment
Diligence
ai-fluency-16.explanation: Deciding how to divide work between humans and AI is the core of Delegation.

ai-fluency-17.question: In that same exercise, asking 'How will I verify the accuracy of the AI's outputs?' belongs to which D?
options: Discernment (and ties into Deployment Diligence upon release)
Delegation
Description
Automation
ai-fluency-17.explanation: Assessing the quality and accuracy of AI outputs is Discernment.

ai-fluency-18.question: Asking 'How will I acknowledge/disclose AI's involvement when publishing the work?' belongs to which D?
options: Diligence (specifically Transparency Diligence)
Delegation
Description
Discernment
ai-fluency-18.explanation: Being transparent about AI's role belongs to the Diligence competency.

ai-fluency-19.question: Which of the following examples best demonstrates 'Augmentation' rather than 'Automation'?
options: Asking AI to act as a critical reviewer to debate with you and refine each argument for a presentation
Giving AI a list of 100 invoices to extract dates into a predefined template
Configuring an agent to automatically monitor email all week without your review
Turning off AI and writing everything manually
ai-fluency-19.explanation: Thinking, debating, and improving ideas together is Augmentation.

ai-fluency-20.question: Which authors collaborated with Anthropic to create the academic framework behind 'AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations'?
options: Rick Dakan and Joseph Feller (released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license)
Alan Turing and John McCarthy
Linus Torvalds and Guido van Rossum
Tim Berners-Lee and Vint Cerf
ai-fluency-20.explanation: The course is based on The AI Fluency Framework by Rick Dakan, Joseph Feller, and Anthropic (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

ai-fluency-21.question: What is the fundamental difference between Traditional AI and Generative AI?
options: Traditional AI analyzes or classifies existing data (e.g., spam filtering), whereas Generative AI can create entirely new content (e.g., drafting a new email)
Traditional AI always runs faster and is smarter than Generative AI at every task
Generative AI can only process numbers, not text
The two types are completely identical
ai-fluency-21.explanation: Generative AI creates new content (text, images, code) rather than only analyzing or labeling existing data.

ai-fluency-22.question: What are the Three Pillars of technology that made the modern Generative AI boom possible?
options: 1) Algorithms (the 2017 Transformer architecture), 2) Data explosion (massive digital data), and 3) Computing power (powerful processors like GPUs)
1) Blockchain, 2) Virtual Reality, and 3) 3G networks
1) Floppy disks, 2) Dot-matrix printers, and 3) Assembly language
1) Paper-only data, 2) Single-core CPUs, and 3) Hand-written if-else rules
ai-fluency-22.explanation: The three pillars are Algorithms (Transformer 2017), Data explosion, and Computing power (GPUs).

ai-fluency-23.question: What is the name of the breakthrough algorithmic architecture introduced in 2017 that enabled LLMs to efficiently process long text sequences?
options: Transformer architecture
Bubble Sort architecture
Relational Database architecture
Client-Server FTP architecture
ai-fluency-23.explanation: The Transformer architecture (2017) revolutionized handling long-range context in natural language.

ai-fluency-24.question: What are the three main stages in the lifecycle of building and operating a Large Language Model (LLM)?
options: Pre-training -> Fine-tuning -> Deployment
Compile -> Link -> Zip
Download -> Print -> Archive
Encrypt -> Hash -> Delete
ai-fluency-24.explanation: Models go through Pre-training (learning patterns from billions of examples), Fine-tuning (learning to follow instructions safely), and Deployment (responding to user prompts).

ai-fluency-25.question: During the 'Pre-training' stage, what does an LLM learn?
options: Analyzing billions of text examples to learn language patterns and predict what comes next
Learning to read each individual user's thoughts via webcam
Memorizing only 100 multiple-choice questions
Automatically installing the Windows operating system
ai-fluency-25.explanation: Pre-training equips the model with broad knowledge and language patterns by predicting the next token.

ai-fluency-26.question: What is the main goal of the 'Fine-tuning' stage after Pre-training?
options: Refining the model to follow user instructions, respond helpfully, and avoid generating harmful content
Erasing all knowledge learned during Pre-training
Doubling the size of image files
Disconnecting the model from all tools
ai-fluency-26.explanation: Fine-tuning transforms a raw text-prediction model into a helpful, instruction-following, and safe assistant.

ai-fluency-27.question: In the 'Deployment' stage, how does the model generate an answer?
options: The user sends a prompt, and the model generates a response based on that prompt combined with patterns learned during training
The model looks up a fixed, pre-written answer table for each question
The model forwards the question to a human staff member to type the answer
The model does not use the user's prompt
ai-fluency-27.explanation: At Deployment, the LLM probabilistically generates dynamic responses based on the input prompt and trained weights.

ai-fluency-28.question: According to the course materials, what are the 4 Key Capabilities of modern Generative AI?
options: Versatile language skills, general-purpose abilities (switching tasks without retraining), learning from examples, and connecting to external tools and data
Always knowing the future 100%, never making math errors, infinite memory, and human consciousness
Only translating English to French
Only running without electricity
ai-fluency-28.explanation: The 4 capabilities are: Versatile language skills, General-purpose abilities, Learning from examples, and Connecting to external tools and data.

ai-fluency-29.question: Which 4 Current Limitations of Generative AI are highlighted in Lesson 3B?
options: Knowledge cutoff date, potential inaccuracies ('hallucinations'), context window constraints, and challenges with complex reasoning and math
Cannot write emails, cannot summarize text, cannot generate code, and cannot understand English
Only works at night
Always takes 1 hour to answer 1 question
ai-fluency-29.explanation: The 4 core limitations are: knowledge cutoff date, hallucinations, context window limits, and difficulty with complex reasoning/math.

ai-fluency-30.question: What does the term 'Hallucination' refer to in Generative AI?
options: When the model produces factually incorrect outputs presented in a very confident and plausible-sounding tone
When the model crashes with a blue screen and outputs no text
When the model refuses to answer an illegal request
When the model automatically translates text into another language
ai-fluency-30.explanation: Hallucination occurs when an LLM fabricates nonexistent facts or citations while maintaining a smooth, convincing style.

ai-fluency-31.question: How does the 'Knowledge cutoff date' affect an LLM's responses?
options: The model does not inherently know events, library versions, or news that occurred after its training data ended (unless connected to external search/data tools)
The model automatically stops working after that date
The model forgets all historical knowledge prior to the year 2000
The model cannot read files uploaded by the user
ai-fluency-31.explanation: A model's internal knowledge is frozen at its cutoff date; accessing newer data requires Web Search, MCP, or RAG.

ai-fluency-32.question: When asking a standalone LLM (with no code-execution tool) to perform a multi-step complex financial calculation, what risk is likely to occur?
options: Calculation or reasoning errors, because LLMs predict tokens probabilistically rather than acting as deterministic arithmetic calculators
The computer's GPU catches fire
The LLM always refuses to do simple addition
The result is always 100% accurate
ai-fluency-32.explanation: One of the 4 LLM limitations is 'Challenges with complex reasoning and math'; using a code-execution tool effectively mitigates this.

ai-fluency-33.question: What benefit do 'Learning from examples' and 'Conversational awareness' provide to users?
options: You can include a few sample examples right in the prompt for the AI to match your desired format/style and iterate over multiple turns without retraining the model
You must retrain the entire model from scratch every time you change your request
You can only ask 1 question before closing the webpage
The AI automatically remembers every other user's conversations
ai-fluency-33.explanation: In-context learning allows AI to adapt flexibly across chat turns simply through examples in the prompt.

ai-fluency-34.question: According to Lesson 3B, how are the most effective AI applications created?
options: By combining the complementary strengths of humans and AI: humans provide critical thinking, judgment, creativity, and ethical oversight
By completely removing humans from the review process
By letting AI freely make legal and medical decisions without approval
By using AI only for the tasks it performs worst at
ai-fluency-34.explanation: Human-AI complementarity: AI handles speed and language scale, while humans provide critical thinking, judgment, creativity, and ethical oversight.

ai-fluency-35.question: Why does understanding Pre-training, Fine-tuning, and Limitations in Deep Dive 1 help with the 'Delegation' competency?
options: It builds 'Platform Awareness'—helping you know what AI is good and weak at so you assign the right tasks and attach the right supporting tools
It helps you assemble GPU chips at home
It means you never need to write prompts again
It completely eliminates Context Window limits
ai-fluency-35.explanation: Understanding technical foundations helps you make smarter Delegation decisions rather than holding misplaced expectations of AI.

ai-fluency-36.question: In Lab 02 (`genai_capabilities_lab.py`), if a task requires looking up today's stock prices with NO external tool, what risk warning does the system flag?
options: HIGH_RISK_CUTOFF — Likely to hit Knowledge Cutoff or Hallucination limits; requires connecting Web Search or MCP
GOOD_FIT — AI always knows today's stock prices without internet access
No risk at all
AI will automatically open the stock exchange
ai-fluency-36.explanation: Real-time data after the cutoff date strictly requires an external retrieval tool.

ai-fluency-37.question: What is the practical impact of 'Context window constraints' when working with extremely long documents?
options: The AI's working memory space is finite; stuffing too much information in at once can cause the AI to miss details in the middle or hit capacity limits
The AI can only read 1 sentence per day
The AI will automatically delete the original file on your machine
There is no impact
ai-fluency-37.explanation: The context window is finite, so information must be managed cleanly and chunked appropriately.

ai-fluency-38.question: Which example accurately illustrates the 'Connecting to external tools and data' capability of modern Generative AI?
options: Claude invokes a web search tool, runs Python code, or connects to an MCP server to read up-to-date data outside its training corpus
Claude fabricates a nonexistent URL
Claude only replies in plain text and never calls functions
The user manually types data into an Excel file
ai-fluency-38.explanation: Connecting to external tools helps LLMs overcome cutoff limits and pure-text arithmetic limitations.

ai-fluency-39.question: Which of the following statements about Generative AI is FALSE?
options: Generative AI always answers 100% of historical and current events accurately without needing verification
Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, and source code
The Transformer (2017) was a major algorithmic breakthrough
Humans must retain the role of critical thinking and ethical oversight
ai-fluency-39.explanation: Generative AI can hallucinate and is constrained by its knowledge cutoff, so human verification is always required.

ai-fluency-40.question: According to Lesson 3B, why is Generative AI more versatile than older specialized AI systems?
options: Because a single general-purpose model can smoothly switch across many language tasks (summarizing, translating, coding, brainstorming) without separate retraining for each task
Because it can only perform a single spam-classification task
Because it requires no training data
Because it operates purely by random chance
ai-fluency-40.explanation: General-purpose abilities allow LLMs to handle diverse tasks simply by changing the prompt.

ai-fluency-41.question: What are the three core components of the 'Delegation' competency (The 4Ds: Delegation)?
options: Problem Awareness, Platform Awareness, and Task Delegation
Product, Process, and Performance
Creation, Transparency, and Deployment
Pre-training, Fine-tuning, and Deployment
ai-fluency-41.explanation: Delegation consists of: Problem Awareness ('What am I trying to do?'), Platform Awareness ('What do you do well?'), and Task Delegation ('OK, here's the plan').

ai-fluency-42.question: What is the central question of 'Problem Awareness' in Delegation?
options: 'What am I trying to do?' — Clearly understanding the goal and nature of the work before bringing AI in
'What do you do well?' — Understanding the strengths of each AI system
'Which font should I use?'
'How many GPUs does the server have?'
ai-fluency-42.explanation: Problem Awareness requires clearly defining the goal, success criteria, and nature of the task before touching AI.

ai-fluency-43.question: What does 'Platform Awareness' in Delegation require from the user?
options: Understanding the capabilities and limitations of different AI systems/models to pick the right tool for the right job
Knowing only a single button in the browser
Rewriting the operating system from scratch
Ignoring AI limitations
ai-fluency-43.explanation: Platform Awareness: 'What do you do well?'—knowing which model excels where and where its limitations lie.

ai-fluency-44.question: What is the goal of the 'Task Delegation' ('OK, here's the plan') step?
options: Thoughtfully dividing work between humans and AI to maximize each party's strengths
Dumping 100% of all work onto AI without reviewing it
Doing 100% manually and banning AI participation
Splitting a file into individual characters
ai-fluency-44.explanation: Task Delegation organizes which parts humans handle, which parts AI handles, and which parts both collaborate on.

ai-fluency-45.question: According to the 'The 4Ds: Delegation' slide, effective Delegation requires a combination of which two factors?
options: Both domain expertise and an understanding of AI capabilities
Only knowing how to write JavaScript code
Only having a paid account
Only asking the shortest possible questions
ai-fluency-45.explanation: 'Effective delegation requires both domain expertise and an understanding of AI capabilities.'

ai-fluency-46.question: In the 'Project planning and delegation' exercise, how should you interact with Claude in Step 3 (Task breakdown)?
options: Engage in a genuine conversation: challenge assumptions and ask clarifying questions about which tasks need human strengths vs. AI, rather than issuing one-way statements
Issue a single command and close the browser immediately
Forbid Claude from asking any follow-up questions
Only work on 10-year projects
ai-fluency-46.explanation: The course emphasizes 'genuine conversation': challenging assumptions, asking clarifying questions, and staying open to unexpected perspectives.

ai-fluency-47.question: What are the three components of the 'Description' competency (The 4Ds: Description)?
options: Product Description, Process Description, and Performance Description
Problem Awareness, Platform Awareness, and Task Delegation
Creation, Transparency, and Deployment
Automation, Augmentation, and Agency
ai-fluency-47.explanation: Description comprises: Product (what), Process (how), and Performance (behavior/attitude during collaboration).

ai-fluency-48.question: What does 'Product Description' define for the AI?
options: Defining WHAT YOU WANT in terms of outputs, format, audience, and style
Defining the step-by-step algorithm the AI must run
Defining the AI's demeanor (such as acting as a Socratic tutor)
Defining company security policies
ai-fluency-48.explanation: Product Description specifies the desired output (don't make the AI guess what you're thinking!).

ai-fluency-49.question: What does 'Process Description' mean when communicating with AI?
options: Defining HOW the AI should approach your request, such as providing step-by-step instructions for it to follow
Only stating the final product name without suggesting how to make it
Specifying the application UI colors
Reviewing the result after the AI has finished
ai-fluency-49.explanation: Process Description guides the thinking/execution workflow (e.g., 'The first thing we need to do...').

ai-fluency-50.question: The example 'Act as a Socratic tutor' (asking guiding questions) belongs to which type of Description?
options: Performance Description (defining the AI's behavior and interaction style during collaboration)
Product Description
Problem Awareness
Deployment Diligence
ai-fluency-50.explanation: Performance Description specifies how the AI should behave while working together (concise vs. detailed, challenging vs. supportive, etc.).

ai-fluency-51.question: According to the PDF '6 Techniques for Effective Prompt Engineering', what are the 6 foundational techniques?
options: 1) Provide context, 2) Show examples of what 'good' looks like, 3) Specify output constraints, 4) Break complex tasks into steps, 5) Ask it to think first, 6) Define the AI's role
1) Write as short as possible, 2) Give no examples, 3) Set no length limits, 4) Merge everything into 1 sentence, 5) Forbid AI from thinking, 6) Define no role
Use only 1 technique: typing in ALL CAPS
Use only Base64 encoding
ai-fluency-51.explanation: The 6 foundational techniques are presented with Before/After examples in the Deep Dive 2 document.

ai-fluency-52.question: In Technique 1 ('Provide context'), what is the difference between the 'Before: Tell me about climate change' prompt and the 'After' prompt?
options: The 'After' prompt specifies scope, geography, timeframe, and asks for examples ('3 major impacts on tropical agriculture over the past decade with examples')
The 'After' prompt shortens it to a single word 'Climate'
The 'After' prompt switches to Latin
There is no difference
ai-fluency-52.explanation: Provide context requires specifying scope, geography, timeframe, and relevant parameters.

ai-fluency-53.question: How does Technique 2 ('Show examples of what "good" looks like') help the AI?
options: Providing sample examples (Before -> After) helps the AI grasp your desired phrasing, style, and format much more clearly than abstract descriptions alone
It confuses the AI so it cannot answer
It eliminates the need to check outputs entirely
It only works for arithmetic problems
ai-fluency-53.explanation: Illustrative examples (few-shot examples) communicate quality standards and formatting more accurately than abstract descriptions.

ai-fluency-54.question: In Technique 3 ('Specify output constraints'), what elements should you clearly specify for the output?
options: Section structure, display format, length, or specific design constraints (e.g., a portfolio page with Hero, About Me, Skills..., sticky nav, sunset palette, dark/light toggle)
Intentionally keeping all constraints secret so the AI guesses
Just writing 'make it pretty'
Forcing the AI to return 10,000 pages
ai-fluency-54.explanation: Specifying format, required sections, length, and constraints ensures the output matches expectations right away.

ai-fluency-55.question: What effect does Technique 4 ('Break complex tasks into steps') have on an AI model?
options: It guides the AI's reasoning along a clear step-by-step path (1, 2, 3, 4), ensuring a thorough and methodical answer
It makes the AI forget the first step
It degrades data analysis quality
It prevents the AI from analyzing trends
ai-fluency-55.explanation: Breaking complex tasks into sequential steps prevents the AI from skipping important aspects.

ai-fluency-56.question: What does Technique 5 ('Ask it to think first') advise you to ask the AI to do before giving its final recommendation?
options: Think carefully through relevant factors, potential constraints, and multiple approaches before settling on the optimal solution
Answer immediately with the very first word that comes to mind
Ignore all practical constraints
Give only a single word: Yes or No
ai-fluency-56.explanation: Giving AI room to think first ('Before answering, please think through...') produces deeper and more comprehensive answers.

ai-fluency-57.question: What does Technique 6 ('Define the AI's role') shape in the AI's response?
options: It shapes the role, tone, and explanation style tailored to a specific audience (e.g., an experienced science teacher explaining to a curious 10-year-old)
It changes the API pricing
It changes network speed
It clears the browser cache
ai-fluency-57.explanation: Defining role/tone/style aligns the response precisely with the reader's level and context.

ai-fluency-58.question: According to the '6 Techniques' PDF, what is the 'Secret Weapon' when you aren't sure how to write a prompt for the best results?
options: Asking the AI for help with prompting (describing your goal and asking Claude to suggest an effective prompt)
Giving up on using AI
Copying someone else's prompt from a completely unrelated field
Typing the exact same question 20 times
ai-fluency-58.explanation: Asking AI to design/improve a prompt for your goal is called the 'Secret Weapon'—perhaps the most powerful technique!

ai-fluency-59.question: In the 'Bad Prompt Makeover' exercise (Lesson 6), you improve a bad prompt by combining which 3 aspects of Description?
options: Product description (what you want), Process description (how Claude should approach it), and Performance description (how Claude should behave while working together)
Only fixing spelling errors in the first word
Only changing periods to exclamation marks
Adding lots of emojis at the end of the sentence
ai-fluency-59.explanation: Remaking a prompt through all 3 lenses—Product, Process, and Performance—turns vague AI interactions into sharp ones.

ai-fluency-60.question: Which statement is true about creating effective prompts in Lesson 7?
options: Successful prompting is iterative and collaborative—expect to refine it gradually based on the AI's responses
A good prompt must be perfect on the very first try and never need editing
You should never ask the AI to revise a prompt
Prompting only applies to programmers
ai-fluency-60.explanation: Prompting is a continuous iterative loop between communication and feedback.

ai-fluency-61.question: According to the 'The 4Ds: Discernment' slide, what are the 3 types of Discernment?
options: Product Discernment, Process Discernment, and Performance Discernment
Product Description, Process Description, and Performance Description
Creation, Transparency, and Deployment
Problem, Platform, and Task
ai-fluency-61.explanation: The 3 types of Discernment parallel the 3 types of Description: Product, Process, and Performance.

ai-fluency-62.question: Which aspect of AI interaction does 'Product Discernment' evaluate?
options: Evaluating the quality of what the AI produced: accuracy, appropriateness, coherence, and relevance
Evaluating whether the AI used a friendly tone
Evaluating whether you should disclose AI usage
Evaluating the user's typing speed
ai-fluency-62.explanation: Product Discernment inspects the quality of the AI's final output.

ai-fluency-63.question: What does 'Process Discernment' focus on checking?
options: Evaluating how the AI arrived at its output: looking for logical errors, lapses in attention, or inappropriate reasoning steps
Evaluating the color of buttons on a webpage
Evaluating whether the AI speaks fast or slow
Evaluating electricity bills
ai-fluency-63.explanation: Process Discernment scrutinizes the reasoning chain and how the AI executed the process you assigned.

ai-fluency-64.question: What does 'Performance Discernment' evaluate while working with AI?
options: Evaluating how the AI behaved throughout its interaction with you and whether its communication style was effective for your needs
Evaluating the server's CPU speed
Evaluating hard drive capacity
Evaluating image copyrights
ai-fluency-64.explanation: Performance Discernment examines the AI's demeanor and collaboration style (e.g., whether it asked good guiding questions or was overly verbose).

ai-fluency-65.question: In Lesson 9, how does 'The Description–Discernment loop' operate?
options: Clear Description -> Receive output -> Discernment (Product/Process/Performance) -> Refine Description & integrate your expertise -> Repeat until standard is met
Write once -> Accept immediately without reading
Evaluate first, then describe the goal afterward
Repeat only if the AI loses network connection
ai-fluency-65.explanation: Description and Discernment form a continuous feedback loop that produces results superior to either humans or AI working alone.

ai-fluency-66.question: In Step 3.4 of the 'Project execution with description-discernment loops' exercise (Lesson 9), what does 'Integrate your own expertise and judgment' require you to do?
options: Add your own perspective, creativity, or domain knowledge; make the final call on what to keep, edit, or discard; and take responsibility for the final product
Let AI make all decisions on what to keep or discard
Delete all personal opinions to keep the AI's text verbatim
Skip reading the final product
ai-fluency-66.explanation: Humans always remain the ones integrating expertise, making final decisions, and taking responsibility.

ai-fluency-67.question: Compared to the first 3 Ds (Delegation, Description, Discernment) which focus on effectiveness and efficiency, what core focus does the fourth D—'Diligence'—address?
options: Ethical and safe aspects—ensuring AI collaboration is responsible, transparent, and trustworthy
Only increasing prompt typing speed
Only reducing word count in answers
Only choosing UI colors
ai-fluency-67.explanation: Diligence shifts focus to ethical responsibility, transparency, and safety verification.

ai-fluency-68.question: What are the three components of 'Diligence' (The 4Ds: Diligence)?
options: Creation Diligence, Transparency Diligence, and Deployment Diligence
Product, Process, and Performance
Automation, Augmentation, and Agency
Algorithms, Data, and Computing power
ai-fluency-68.explanation: The 3 pillars of Diligence are Creation (when creating), Transparency (when disclosing), and Deployment (when releasing/using).

ai-fluency-69.question: What responsibility does 'Creation Diligence' refer to when working with AI?
options: Being thoughtful and intentional about which AI system you choose to use and how you interact with it (e.g., protecting private/sensitive data, avoiding copyright infringement)
Freely pasting all passwords and confidential customer data into any public chatbot
Using only AI models from unknown sources
Ignoring intellectual property rights
ai-fluency-69.explanation: Creation Diligence: carefully choosing an appropriate AI system and providing data/interacting responsibly.

ai-fluency-70.question: What does 'Transparency Diligence' require?
options: Being honest and transparent about AI's role in your work with everyone who needs to know (depending on personal, academic, or professional context)
Completely hiding AI usage even when an organization requires disclosure
Claiming 100% credit for fully AI-generated work as entirely handwritten when submitting assignments
Publishing your secret API keys online
ai-fluency-70.explanation: Transparency Diligence: being honest about the extent of AI's contribution with relevant stakeholders.

ai-fluency-71.question: What does 'Deployment Diligence' mean?
options: Taking responsibility for verifying and vouching for the AI outputs that you use or share externally
Pushing unverified AI outputs straight to production or sending them to clients
Blaming the AI company entirely if your product has errors
Testing once and ignoring errors
ai-fluency-71.explanation: If you put a product into use or share it, you are the one verifying and vouching for its quality.

ai-fluency-72.question: Why do different contexts (personal, academic, professional) have different expectations for Diligence?
options: Because disclosure and verification requirements vary by environment (e.g., personal notes differ from university theses or medical/enterprise reports)
Because AI does not work in academic environments
Because only personal environments require ethics
There is no difference across contexts
ai-fluency-72.explanation: Standards and rules for disclosure and verification change depending on personal, academic, or professional context.

ai-fluency-73.question: In the 'Creating a Diligence Statement' exercise (Lesson 10), what is a 'Diligence Statement'?
options: A transparent statement acknowledging AI's role in your work, demonstrating careful verification, and explaining your ethical choices
A Python snippet used to shut down a server
An internet billing invoice
A request for AI to write a paper without you reading it
ai-fluency-73.explanation: A Diligence Statement helps readers, colleagues, or instructors see clearly where AI assisted and how you verified and took responsibility.

ai-fluency-74.question: When reflecting on 'Transparency Diligence' while writing a Diligence Statement, which question do you need to answer?
options: Who needs to know about my AI usage? How should I present it honestly, and what level of detail is appropriate for each part of the work?
How can I hide it so nobody notices?
How many colors can I use in the slides?
How many gigabytes is the AI model?
ai-fluency-74.explanation: Transparency Diligence considers the right audience who needs to know and the appropriate level of transparency.

ai-fluency-75.question: When reflecting on 'Deployment Diligence', what is the most central question?
options: What steps did I take to verify the accuracy/appropriateness of AI content? Did I check for errors, bias, or omissions? How confident am I in vouching for the final product?
Did the AI write it in under 2 seconds?
How many tokens did I spend?
What percentage of battery is left on my computer?
ai-fluency-75.explanation: Deployment Diligence requires a substantive verification process before vouching for the output.

ai-fluency-76.question: In Lesson 11 ('Conclusion'), what does the 'Build a Personal AI Policy' exercise help you define?
options: Defining contexts where you use AI, boundaries where you don't, output verification workflows, sensitive data handling, transparency templates, and impact on others
Only picking a favorite background color for the chat UI
Listing social media account passwords
Deleting all previous lessons
ai-fluency-76.explanation: A Personal AI Policy serves as a personal/professional compass for consistently applying the 4D Framework.

ai-fluency-77.question: According to Lesson 11 Key Takeaways, when does human-AI collaboration produce the strongest results?

When humans delegate completely without oversight
When humans refuse to use any AI tools
When using AI only in Automation mode for every creative problem

ai-fluency-78.question: In Lab 04 (`discernment_diligence_lab.py`), if an AI response has `has_unverified_claim: True` and `followed_all_steps: False`, which types of Discernment does the system flag?

It marks it 100% compliant and allows immediate release
It only flags a network error
It automatically deletes the data

ai-fluency-79.question: What is the correct relationship among the 4 Ds across the entire course?

Only do Diligence and skip the other 3 Ds
Description has nothing to do with Discernment
Delegation is the final step after releasing the product

ai-fluency-80.question: What is the final takeaway of 'AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations' regarding the future of your skills?
options: AI Fluency develops through practice; every AI interaction is an opportunity to practice the 4Ds to stay effective, efficient, ethical, and safe as technology evolves
Once you finish this course, you never need to practice again
Just memorize the names of the 4 Ds without applying them in practice
AI will automatically assume all legal responsibility on behalf of users

mcp-advanced-1.question: What is Sampling in MCP?
options: A mechanism that allows an MCP server to ask the client to call an AI model (Claude) on its behalf
A mechanism to randomly sample data from a database
A mechanism to compress server logs
A mechanism for the client to sample the list of tools
mcp-advanced-1.explanation: Sampling lets the server request that the client execute an LLM call and return the result.

mcp-advanced-2.question: What main problem does Sampling solve?
options: A server needs AI capabilities without wanting to integrate a model itself, hold API keys, or pay token costs
The client downloads files too slowly
The server cannot run tools synchronously
Lack of a user authentication method
mcp-advanced-2.explanation: The server offloads calling Claude to the client so it doesn't need its own API key or AI integration.

mcp-advanced-3.question: In the Sampling flow, who actually calls Claude?
options: The client (after receiving a sampling request from the server)
The server using its own API key
An Anthropic proxy embedded in MCP
The user manually
mcp-advanced-3.explanation: The server sends a sampling request; the client calls Claude and returns the result.

mcp-advanced-4.question: Who bears the token cost when using Sampling?
options: The client (which calls Claude), not the server
The server
The transport provider
Nobody, it is free
mcp-advanced-4.explanation: Benefit: cost and responsibility shift to the client.

mcp-advanced-5.question: On the server side (Python SDK), which method sends a sampling request?
options: ctx.session.create_message(...)
ctx.sample_ai(...)
session.call_claude(...)
mcp.ask_client(...)
mcp-advanced-5.explanation: The server uses `create_message` with a list of SamplingMessage, max_tokens, system_prompt, etc.

mcp-advanced-6.question: What does the client need to provide to support Sampling?
options: sampling_callback passed into ClientSession
logging_callback passed into call_tool
A roots.json file
The environment variable SAMPLING=1
mcp-advanced-6.explanation: The client defines `sampling_callback` and passes it when creating ClientSession.

mcp-advanced-7.question: What data type does the client's sampling_callback return?
options: CreateMessageResult (role assistant, model, content)
A raw JSON string
ListRootsResult
InitializeResult
mcp-advanced-7.explanation: The callback returns `CreateMessageResult` containing the content generated by Claude.

mcp-advanced-8.question: In which scenario is Sampling most useful?
options: A public MCP server where you do not control the client
When you control both the server and the client
When the server runs via STDIO on a single personal machine
When no AI is being used
mcp-advanced-8.explanation: For public servers, sampling lets the server use AI without needing its own API key.

mcp-advanced-9.question: When you control both the server and the client, which statement is reasonable?
options: Sampling is usually unnecessary because the server can integrate AI directly
Sampling is mandatory
Sampling is prohibited
Roots must be used instead
mcp-advanced-9.explanation: Sampling primarily solves the problem of a server not wanting to integrate AI itself.

mcp-advanced-10.question: Does an MCP server using Sampling need an Anthropic API key?
options: No, because the client will call Claude
Yes, always
Only when using STDIO
Only when using Roots
mcp-advanced-10.explanation: The server needs no key—that is one of the main benefits.

mcp-advanced-11.question: What is the purpose of log and progress notifications?
options: To let users know what is happening while a long-running tool executes
To encrypt data
To replace the tool result
To authenticate the client
mcp-advanced-11.explanation: They prevent the feeling of a frozen app by providing real-time feedback.

mcp-advanced-12.question: In the Python MCP SDK, through which object does a tool access logging/progress?
options: Context (the automatically provided ctx parameter)
Global variable LOGGER
ClientSession
Roots
mcp-advanced-12.explanation: Context provides methods such as ctx.info() and ctx.report_progress().

mcp-advanced-13.question: What arguments does ctx.report_progress(...) accept?
options: Current progress and total
Only a message string
The client name
A list of roots

mcp-advanced-14.question: Where is the callback that receives log messages passed on the client?
options: logging_callback when creating ClientSession
call_tool(progress_callback=...)
initialize()
list_roots()
mcp-advanced-14.explanation: logging_callback is passed when creating the session; progress_callback is passed when calling a tool.

mcp-advanced-15.question: Where is progress_callback passed on the client?
options: When calling session.call_tool(..., progress_callback=...)
When creating ClientSession
In the config file
When calling initialize
mcp-advanced-15.explanation: Progress is tied to each specific tool call.

mcp-advanced-16.question: Is implementing notifications mandatory?
options: No, it is completely optional—the client may ignore them
Mandatory per specification
Mandatory for STDIO
Mandatory for StreamableHTTP
mcp-advanced-16.explanation: They are solely for improving user experience.

mcp-advanced-17.question: How should a Web application present progress/logs?
options: WebSocket, server-sent events, or polling to push updates to the browser
Print to the server's terminal
They cannot be displayed
Send an email
mcp-advanced-17.explanation: CLI: print to terminal; Web: WebSocket/SSE/polling; Desktop: progress bar.

mcp-advanced-18.question: What are Roots used for in MCP?
options: Granting the server access to specific files or folders
Specifying the Python installation directory
Declaring network ports
Storing tool schemas
mcp-advanced-18.explanation: Roots allow users to grant a server access to specific paths.

mcp-advanced-19.question: Without Roots, what problem occurs for file-processing tools (e.g., video conversion)?
options: The server doesn't know where to look for files and the user cannot control the access scope
The tool runs faster
There is no problem
Claude automatically remembers every path
mcp-advanced-19.explanation: Roots define the allowed area for searching and access.

mcp-advanced-20.question: Does the MCP Python SDK automatically enforce roots boundaries?
options: No—you must implement checks yourself (e.g., is_path_allowed) before reading or writing files
Yes, completely automatically
Only when using StreamableHTTP
Only when json_response is enabled
mcp-advanced-20.explanation: A helper function is needed to verify that a path lies within the granted roots.

mcp-advanced-21.question: What is the correct sequence of Roots in Action?
options: User requests -> Claude calls tool with path -> server checks path is within roots -> performs operation
Server performs operation -> then asks user
Client uploads the entire disk to the server
Claude automatically deletes files outside roots
mcp-advanced-21.explanation: The roots check happens before performing the file operation.

mcp-advanced-22.question: What are the main benefits of Roots?
options: User control over access, focused search, increased security, and flexibility
Faster network speed
Replacing Sampling
Automatic file encryption
mcp-advanced-22.explanation: Roots: user control, focused search, security, flexibility.

mcp-advanced-23.question: Where are MCP's JSON messages officially defined?
options: TypeScript schema in the official MCP specification repository
In a .proto file
In each server's own OpenAPI YAML
There is no official definition
mcp-advanced-23.explanation: The MCP specification defines messages using a TypeScript schema.

mcp-advanced-24.question: Why does the MCP specification use TypeScript?
options: As a schema language to describe message types; using TypeScript for implementation is not required
Because MCP only runs on Node.js
Because clients must be written in TypeScript
Because TypeScript is faster than Python
mcp-advanced-24.explanation: TypeScript is used solely as a way to describe the schema.

mcp-advanced-25.question: Into which two major groups are MCP messages divided?
options: Request–Result and Notification
Sync and Async
Tool and Prompt
Public and Private
mcp-advanced-25.explanation: A Request always has a Result; a Notification does not.

mcp-advanced-26.question: Which of the following pairs is a Request–Result?
options: Call Tool Request -> Call Tool Result
Progress Notification -> Result
Logging Message -> Result
Tool List Changed -> Result
mcp-advanced-26.explanation: Examples of pairs: Call Tool, List Prompts, Read Resource, Initialize...

mcp-advanced-27.question: How does a Notification differ from a Request?
options: It does not require a response
It always contains an API key
It is only sent by the client
It always uses SSE
mcp-advanced-27.explanation: A Notification is a one-way message that does not require a Result.

mcp-advanced-28.question: Which of the following is an example of a Notification?
options: Progress, Logging Message, Tool List Changed, Resource Updated
Call Tool Request
Initialize Request
Read Resource Request

mcp-advanced-29.question: Which of the following messages is sent from the SERVER to the CLIENT?
options: Create Message Request (sampling) and List Roots Request
Call Tool Request
List Tools Request
Initialize Request
mcp-advanced-29.explanation: Sampling and roots are server->client requests.

mcp-advanced-30.question: Which messages are sent from the CLIENT to the SERVER?
options: Call Tool, List Tools, Read Resource, Initialize
Create Message Request
List Roots Request
Progress Notification
mcp-advanced-30.explanation: Operations that 'use' the server are initiated by the client.

mcp-advanced-31.question: Why is it important to understand message types before choosing a transport?
options: Because some transports (StreamableHTTP) restrict server->client messages
Because all transports are identical
Because it only relates to security
Because it only relates to Roots
mcp-advanced-31.explanation: HTTP limitations affect which message types can be used.

mcp-advanced-32.question: How does the STDIO transport work?
options: The client launches the server as a child process and communicates via stdin/stdout
Via HTTP POST to a remote server
Via WebSocket
Via a shared file
mcp-advanced-32.explanation: The server runs as a subprocess of the client.

mcp-advanced-33.question: What is a communication characteristic of STDIO?
options: Full bidirectional—the server can send messages at any time
Only the client can send
Requires mcp-session-id
Requires an SSE workaround
mcp-advanced-33.explanation: STDIO does not have HTTP's limitations.

mcp-advanced-34.question: When is STDIO most suitable?
options: When the client and server run on the same machine
When the server is remote over the Internet
When horizontal scaling is needed
When a load balancer is needed
mcp-advanced-34.explanation: STDIO is used for local environments.

mcp-advanced-35.question: What 3 steps make up the MCP initialization sequence?
options: Initialize Request -> Initialize Result -> Initialized Notification
Hello -> Ack -> Bye
Auth -> Token -> Ready
List Tools -> Call Tool -> Result
mcp-advanced-35.explanation: Client sends Initialize, server returns Result, client sends Initialized Notification.

mcp-advanced-36.question: How are the four communication scenarios (client->server request, server->client result, server->client request, client->server result) supported by STDIO?
options: All of them are supported
Only scenarios 1 and 2
Only when json_response is enabled
None of them
mcp-advanced-36.explanation: STDIO permits communication in all directions.

mcp-advanced-37.question: When is the StreamableHTTP transport used?
options: When the client and server are on different machines (remote server)
When running on the same machine as a subprocess
Only during testing
Only when there is no network
mcp-advanced-37.explanation: Used for remote servers over HTTP.

mcp-advanced-38.question: What is the core limitation of HTTP for MCP?
options: The server cannot proactively send requests to the client
The client cannot send requests
HTTP cannot carry JSON
HTTP has no headers
mcp-advanced-38.explanation: HTTP follows a client-request, server-response model.

mcp-advanced-39.question: Which message types are affected by that limitation?
options: Server->client requests (sampling, list roots) and notifications (logging, progress, etc.)
Call Tool Request
Initialize Request
List Tools Request
mcp-advanced-39.explanation: Server-initiated messages need a reverse channel.

mcp-advanced-40.question: Through what mechanism does StreamableHTTP overcome this limitation?
options: A workaround using Server-Sent Events (SSE)
Mandatory WebSocket
Polling every second
Running STDIO alongside it
mcp-advanced-40.explanation: SSE allows the server to push data to the client.

mcp-advanced-41.question: Which header identifies a session in StreamableHTTP?
options: mcp-session-id
x-api-key
authorization-session
x-mcp-root
mcp-advanced-41.explanation: The server returns mcp-session-id in the Initialize Result.

mcp-advanced-42.question: What does the StreamableHTTP connection initialization sequence consist of?
options: Initialize Request -> server returns Initialize Result + mcp-session-id -> Initialized Notification
GET /session -> POST /token
WebSocket handshake
Just calling a tool directly

mcp-advanced-43.question: With which request does the client open the main SSE connection?
options: GET request
DELETE request
PUT request
OPTIONS request
mcp-advanced-43.explanation: GET opens the SSE stream so the server can push messages.

mcp-advanced-44.question: When calling a tool via POST, how does the SSE workaround behave?
options: An additional SSE stream can be opened for the tool call, creating dual SSE connections
Closes all SSE streams
Switches to STDIO
Terminates the session
mcp-advanced-44.explanation: Dual SSE: main SSE + SSE tied to the tool call.

mcp-advanced-45.question: Through which channel do notifications/requests tied to a tool call typically travel?
options: That tool call's own SSE stream
STDIO
HTTP headers
A log file
mcp-advanced-45.explanation: Independent notifications travel over the main SSE stream.

mcp-advanced-46.question: Which two FastMCP configuration flags break the SSE workaround?
options: stateless_http=True and json_response=True
debug=True and verbose=True
stdio=False and sse=False
cache=True and retry=True

mcp-advanced-47.question: What does json_response=True do?
options: Returns a standard JSON response instead of an SSE stream
Enables encryption
Enables session id
Enables sampling

mcp-advanced-48.question: What does stateless_http=True mean?
options: The server retains no session, issues no mcp-session-id, and the client does not need to initialize beforehand
The server retains sessions longer
Forces STDIO usage
Automatically enables Roots

mcp-advanced-49.question: When stateless HTTP is enabled, which features are lost?
options: Sampling, progress, logging, and subscriptions (all server->client features)
Call Tool
List Tools
Read Resource
mcp-advanced-49.explanation: Only the pure request-response model remains.

mcp-advanced-50.question: Why does production need stateless mode?
options: Behind a load balancer with multiple servers, a subsequent request may hit a different server that does not hold the session
Because stateless is faster than STDIO
Because HTTP forbids sessions
Because SSE is blocked by browsers

mcp-advanced-51.question: What is the problem with a stateful configuration when there are multiple server instances?
options: Sessions/SSE are tied to a specific server, so requests hitting another server will fail
Tools cannot run
There is no JSON
There is no Initialize
mcp-advanced-51.explanation: Stateful requires the client to always hit the exact same server.

mcp-advanced-52.question: With stateless HTTP, does the client need to send an Initialize Request first?
options: Not required
Always required
Only the first time each day
Only for async tools
mcp-advanced-52.explanation: There is no session to establish.

mcp-advanced-53.question: Which code snippet enables stateless + JSON response?
options: FastMCP("name", stateless_http=True, json_response=True)
FastMCP("name").stateless()
mcp.run(mode="stateless")
FastMCP("name", stdio=False)
mcp-advanced-53.explanation: Both flags are passed to the FastMCP constructor.

mcp-advanced-54.question: Which method returns the StreamableHTTP ASGI app to run with an HTTP server?
options: mcp.streamable_http_app()
mcp.stdio_app()
mcp.wsgi()
mcp.build_http()

mcp-advanced-55.question: What should a remote application needing sampling and progress notifications choose?
options: StreamableHTTP stateful (default)
stateless_http=True
json_response=True
HTTP cannot be used
mcp-advanced-55.explanation: Requires the SSE workaround and sessions.

mcp-advanced-56.question: Which transport should a local MCP server launched by the client use?
options: STDIO
StreamableHTTP stateless
SSE only
WebSocket

mcp-advanced-57.question: What should a horizontally scaled remote server behind a load balancer that does not need server->client communication choose?
options: StreamableHTTP with stateless_http=True (and json_response=True)
STDIO
StreamableHTTP stateful with sticky sessions at all times
Use no transport

mcp-advanced-58.question: Which statement about the capability matrix is TRUE?
options: STDIO and StreamableHTTP stateful fully support server->client; stateless HTTP does not
Stateless HTTP supports sampling
STDIO does not support progress
json_response=True enables subscriptions

mcp-advanced-59.question: In Lab 03, with recommend(local=False, need_server_to_client=False, behind_load_balancer=True), what is the result?
options: StreamableHTTP with stateless_http=True, json_response=True
STDIO
StreamableHTTP stateful
No recommendation
mcp-advanced-59.explanation: Remote + load balancer + no reverse channel -> stateless.

mcp-advanced-60.question: Course summary: what is the right formula for choosing features and transport?
options: Use Sampling/Notifications/Roots when needed; local -> STDIO; remote needing reverse channel -> StreamableHTTP stateful; horizontal scaling without reverse channel -> stateless
Always use stateless
Always use STDIO for remote
Never use Roots
mcp-advanced-60.explanation: Choose based on feature requirements and deployment architecture.

subagents-1.question: How are Subagents in Claude Code most accurately defined?
options: Specialized AI assistants to which Claude Code can delegate tasks in an isolated context window, returning only a summary to the main thread
UI plugins used solely to change the colors of the Terminal window
An SQL database used to store user passwords and API keys
A feature that automatically shares your entire chat history to public GitHub
subagents-1.explanation: Subagents are specialized assistants delegated tasks by Claude Code (Parent Agent). Each subagent runs in an isolated context window, independently performs file reads/searches/tool calls, and returns only a concise summary to the main conversation.

subagents-2.question: What core problem occurs with the Main Context Window when you work long-term with Claude Code WITHOUT using Subagents?
options: Every tool call, read file content, and search result accumulates in the finite Main Context Window, causing it to fill up quickly and making Claude gradually lose track of earlier parts of the conversation
Claude Code will automatically wipe the computer's hard drive after every 10 messages
The Main Context Window does not support reading source code files written in Python
The main context window will automatically shrink to 10 tokens after 5 minutes
subagents-2.explanation: The space of the Main Context Window is finite. When all file reads, searches, and tool calls pile up here, the context becomes polluted (context pollution/rot), and as it fills up, Claude starts forgetting important information from the beginning of the conversation.

subagents-3.question: When Claude Code launches a new Subagent, what are the 2 core components that its initial context window receives?
options: 1) A Custom System Prompt from the configuration file defining the subagent's role/behavior, and 2) A Task Description written by the Parent Agent based on the user's request
1) 100% of the entire chat history from the start of the Main Conversation session, and 2) All files in the operating system directory
1) Chat history of all other sibling Subagents, and 2) The system password file
1) Only the user's name, and 2) A list of favorite websites in the browser
subagents-3.explanation: According to Chapter 1 documentation, each subagent starts in an isolated context with: (1) A custom system prompt from the configuration file defining its role & behavior, and (2) A task description written by the Parent Agent based on what you asked for.

subagents-4.question: After a Subagent completes a series of file reads, searches, and processing steps, what information is sent back to the Main Conversation?
options: Only a concise summary of the results is returned to the main conversation
The entire raw content of every file that the Subagent opened and read along the way
All system error logs and binary code of the invoked tools
No information is returned at all; the user must manually open the log file to read it
subagents-4.explanation: The greatest strength of a subagent is its 'one-way valve' mechanism: all intermediate steps (file reads, searches, tool calls) are kept isolated, and upon completion, only the summary returns to the Main Conversation.

subagents-5.question: How does Claude Code handle the detailed conversation and intermediate working steps of a Subagent (which are not brought back to the Main Context)?
options: Claude Code saves the rest of the Subagent's detailed conversation to a separate transcript file
Claude Code emails the entire log to the network administrator
Claude Code stuffs everything into the operating system's PATH environment variable
Claude Code directly overwrites the project's README.md file
subagents-5.explanation: Although only a summary returns to the Main Conversation, Claude Code still saves the full detailed conversation history of the subagent into a separate transcript file.

subagents-6.question: What is the main tradeoff when using a Subagent to keep the Main Context Window clean?
options: The main conversation does not see the detailed process/steps the Subagent took to reach its final conclusions
The Subagent is completely unable to read any files on the hard drive
When using a Subagent, the Main Agent is permanently locked and cannot chat with the user anymore
A Subagent always takes 100 times longer for any question under 5 words
subagents-6.explanation: In Chapter 1 ('Why Subagents Matter'), the documentation clearly states: 'The tradeoff is that your main conversation doesn't see how the subagent reached its conclusions' — the main thread receives a clean answer without seeing the intermediate journey the subagent took.

subagents-7.question: In the Chapter 1 Practical Example, when you want to find which file handles authentication in an unfamiliar codebase and have to read through 15 files to find it, what happens if you delegate this task to the `Explore` Subagent?
options: The Main Context Window only records the question and the summary answer — it does NOT store the contents of the 15 files read during the search
All 15 files are copied into the Main Context Window for the user to inspect line by line
The `Explore` Subagent automatically deletes the 14 unrelated files from the project's hard drive
The `Explore` Subagent refuses to run because it is only allowed to read a maximum of 2 files
subagents-7.explanation: When using the `Explore` subagent, it digs through the 15 files in its own isolated context and returns a focused answer. The Main Context Window only stores the question and the result summary, saving thousands of main context tokens.

subagents-8.question: Which 3 Built-in Subagents does Claude Code ship with out of the box?
options: General-purpose subagent, Explore, and Plan
Frontend-builder, Database-admin, and DevOps-deployer
Compiler, Debugger, and Package-manager
Git-pusher, Docker-runner, and Browser-scraper
subagents-8.explanation: According to the 'Built-in Subagents' section in Chapter 1, Claude Code ships with 3 built-in subagents: (1) General-purpose subagent, (2) Explore, and (3) Plan.

subagents-9.question: Among Claude Code's Built-in Subagents, what is the `Explore` subagent specifically designed for?
options: Fast searching and navigation of codebases
Automatically rewriting the entire Git history and force-pushing to the main branch
Executing database deletion scripts in the Production environment
Simultaneously editing 100 source code files without reading their contents
subagents-9.explanation: `Explore` is a built-in subagent specialized for fast searching and navigation in codebases (typically using read-only tools to maintain safety and high speed).

subagents-10.question: Which Built-in Subagent in Claude Code is designed for multi-step tasks that require BOTH exploration and action?
options: General-purpose subagent
Explore subagent
Plan subagent
Read-only subagent
subagents-10.explanation: The `General-purpose subagent` is a versatile subagent used for multi-step tasks that need to combine both exploration and execution/action.

subagents-11.question: When is the `Plan` Built-in Subagent used by Claude Code?
options: Used in plan mode to research and analyze the codebase before presenting a plan
Only used after the application has been successfully deployed to the cloud
Used to automatically pay monthly AWS service bills
Used to compile C++ source code into machine code
subagents-11.explanation: According to Chapter 1: The `Plan` subagent is used in `plan mode` to perform isolated codebase research and analysis before synthesizing and presenting a plan to the user.

subagents-12.question: Beyond Built-in Subagents, users can create `Custom Subagents` by customizing which core elements?
options: Customizing System Prompts and Tool Access to fit specific workflows
Modifying neural network weights on Anthropic's servers
Changing the TCP/IP protocol of the Windows operating system
Rewriting the Linux kernel compiler in assembly language
subagents-12.explanation: Custom Subagents allow you to define specialized assistants (code reviewer, test writer, documentation generator, etc.) with Custom System Prompts and Custom Tool Access.

subagents-13.question: What are the 3 Key Takeaways (benefits) that Subagents provide according to the summary at the end of Chapter 1?
options: 1) Break work into focused pieces, 2) Keep the Main Context Window clean by isolating intermediate work, 3) Bring back just the information needed as a concise summary
1) Increase physical RAM capacity, 2) Reduce hard drive usage, 3) Automatically upgrade Internet bandwidth speed
1) Completely eliminate the need for System Prompts, 2) Allow API calls without Internet, 3) Automatically fix hardware failures
1) Merge all files into a single file, 2) Save all search logs into the Main Context, 3) Completely disable tool permission checks
subagents-13.explanation: The 3 core benefits of Subagents in the Chapter 1 Key Takeaways are: (1) Break work into focused pieces, (2) Keep your main context window clean by isolating intermediate work, and (3) Bring back just the information you need as a concise summary.

subagents-14.question: When a Subagent is executing file read (`Read`) and search (`Grep`) commands, where do the outputs returned from those tools appear?
options: Completely inside that Subagent's own Context Window (and recorded in its own separate transcript file)
Inserted directly into the middle of the Main Context Window's chat history immediately
Written straight to the user's keyboard clipboard memory
Deleted immediately before the Subagent can even read them
subagents-14.explanation: All intermediate tool call results of a subagent go only into that subagent's own context window for it to read and analyze, without polluting the Main Context Window at all.

subagents-15.question: Who is responsible for writing the initial `task description` to launch a Subagent when delegating work?
options: The Parent Agent (in the main conversation thread) automatically writes it based on the user's request
The graphics card driver (GPU Driver) randomly generates it
The ISP's DNS system
The Subagent writes the question for itself before being called
subagents-15.explanation: According to Chapter 1: When a subagent is launched, it receives 'A task description written by the parent agent based on what you asked for'.

subagents-16.question: Why does minimizing noise in the Main Context Window help during long Claude Code sessions?
options: The less redundant intermediate data in the main context, the better Claude maintains focus, remembers core instructions longer, and works more effectively throughout long sessions
Because Claude Code only allows running a maximum of 3 commands if Subagents are not used
Because the Main Context Window can only store uppercase English letters
Because it reduces the computer monitor's power consumption by 90%
subagents-16.explanation: 'The less noise in your main context, the longer and more effectively you can work' — keeping the Main Context clean prevents attention dilution and avoids hitting context limits too early.

subagents-17.question: What is a Custom Subagent created specifically to inspect source code quality, find potential bugs, and identify security vulnerabilities commonly called?
options: A code reviewer subagent
A billing manager subagent
A DNS resolver subagent
A hardware overclocking subagent
subagents-17.explanation: Code Reviewer is one of the most classic examples of a Custom Subagent mentioned throughout the course (alongside Test Writer and Documentation Generator).

subagents-18.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE about how Subagents work?
options: Subagents share 100% of the Context Window memory with the Main Conversation, so every file a Subagent reads bloats the Main Context
Each Subagent runs in its own independent Context Window
A Subagent returns a concise summary to the main conversation thread upon completion
Claude Code includes both Built-in Subagents and the ability to create Custom Subagents
subagents-18.explanation: The first statement is FALSE because the most fundamental point of a Subagent is running in an INDEPENDENT Context Window so that it does NOT bloat the Main Context.

subagents-19.question: In Lab 01 (`subagent_context_isolation.py`), when comparing reading 15 files directly in the Main Context versus delegating to an `Explore` Subagent, what do the measurements show?
options: The Main Context using the `Explore` Subagent contains only 2 messages (Question + Result Summary), reducing noisy tokens by over 95% compared to reading 15 files directly in the main thread
The Main Context using a Subagent becomes twice as large as without using a Subagent
Both approaches store all 15 files in the Main Context with the exact same token count
The `Explore` Subagent fails to find the file `src/auth/security.py`
subagents-19.explanation: In Lab 01, isolating 15 `Read` calls into the Subagent Context allows the Main Context to retain only the question and final summary, eliminating over 95% of intermediate tokens from the main thread.

subagents-20.question: When can you start using the Built-in Subagents (`General-purpose`, `Explore`, `Plan`) in Claude Code?
options: Right away, because they are already built into Claude Code without needing to create any configuration files
Only after you manually write at least 10 YAML configuration files in the project directory
Only after you install a local PostgreSQL database on your machine
Only after you recompile Claude Code's source code from scratch
subagents-20.explanation: 'Claude Code ships with several built-in subagents you can use right away' — you can use the 3 built-in subagents immediately with no extra configuration required.

subagents-21.question: In what file format are Custom Subagents in Claude Code stored?
options: Markdown files (`.md`) with YAML Frontmatter at the top holding configuration and a body below containing the System Prompt
Encrypted executable binary files (`.exe` or `.dll`)
Microsoft Excel spreadsheets (`.xlsx`)
Vector graphics image files (`.svg`)
subagents-21.explanation: According to Chapter 2: 'They are defined as markdown files with YAML frontmatter that holds the configuration and a body that describes how the subagent should behave.'

subagents-22.question: According to Chapter 2, what is the easiest way to create a Custom Subagent in the Claude Code CLI?
options: Use the `/agents` wizard (`the /agents wizard`) and describe what you want so Claude generates the configuration file for you
Write a C++ program to generate binary code for the agent
Directly edit the Windows operating system Registry
Submit a technical support ticket to Anthropic asking them to create the file for you
subagents-22.explanation: The easiest way is to use the `/agents` command in the Claude Code CLI: the interactive wizard guides you through choosing Scope, Tools, Model, Color, and can let Claude automatically generate `name`, `description`, and `system prompt` from your brief description.

subagents-23.question: When creating a Subagent at the `Project-level` scope, in which directory is its configuration file saved?
options: `.claude/agents/` (inside the root directory of the current project)
`~/.claude/agents/` (in the user's Home directory)
`/etc/claude/system_agents/`
`node_modules/.bin/agents/`
subagents-23.explanation: A Project-level subagent is saved as a `.md` file inside the project's `.claude/agents/` directory and is only available within the current project (and can be committed to Git to share with the team).

subagents-24.question: When you want to create a personal Subagent that can be shared across ALL projects on your computer (`User-level`), where must the configuration file be placed?
options: `~/.claude/agents/` (in the user's Home directory)
`.claude/agents/` (only inside a single project subdirectory)
`/tmp/agents/` (a temporary directory cleared on reboot)
`./tests/fixtures/agents/`
subagents-24.explanation: A User-level subagent is stored at `~/.claude/agents/`, allowing you to share and reuse that subagent across every project on your computer.

subagents-25.question: In the `/agents` wizard, when choosing how to initialize the configuration content after selecting Scope, what does the 'Generate with Claude' (generation wizard) feature do?
options: You simply enter a short description of what you want, and Claude automatically generates the `name`, `description`, and `system prompt` based on that input
It automatically downloads random source code from the Internet without asking you
It deletes all existing subagents in the project
It only changes the font of the Terminal window
subagents-25.explanation: With the `/agents` generation wizard, you just briefly describe the subagent's purpose, and Claude automatically drafts an accurate `name`, `description`, and detailed `system prompt` for you.

subagents-26.question: In the `Customizing Tools` step of the `/agents` wizard, into which 5 categories are the tools grouped?
options: Read-only tools, Edit tools, Execution tools, MCP tools, and Other tools
Audio tools, Video tools, 3D CAD tools, Printing tools, and Gaming tools
SQL tools, NoSQL tools, Graph tools, Vector tools, and Cache tools
Windows tools, Linux tools, macOS tools, iOS tools, and Android tools
subagents-26.explanation: According to Chapter 2 ('Customizing Tools'), the wizard groups tools into 5 clear categories: Read-only tools, Edit tools, Execution tools, MCP tools, and Other tools.

subagents-27.question: Why should you uncheck the `Edit tools` category for a `code-reviewer` subagent?
options: Because a Code Reviewer only needs to read and analyze code; removing Edit permissions prevents the subagent from accidentally modifying your source code during a review
Because if Edit tools are enabled, Claude Code cannot read Markdown files
Because Edit tools turn the subagent's `color` to black
Because Anthropic charges 10x more for every subagent with Edit tools enabled
subagents-27.explanation: 'A code reviewer probably only needs read-only tools. Unchecking edit or execution tools it doesn't need prevents it from modifying code.' — Granting only the necessary tools ensures complete safety.

subagents-28.question: When configuring the `model` field for a Subagent, what are the 4 valid options?
options: `haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`, and `inherit`
`gpt-4`, `llama-3`, `mistral`, and `default`
`small`, `medium`, `large`, and `xlarge`
subagents-28.explanation: The four options for a subagent's `model` field in Claude Code are: `haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`, or `inherit`.

subagents-29.question: Among the `model` options for a Subagent, when should you choose `haiku`, `sonnet`, or `opus`?
options: `haiku` is best for fast, lightweight tasks; `sonnet` is a good balance between speed and depth; `opus` is best for complex analysis
`haiku` is for the most complex architectural analysis; `opus` is only for ultra-lightweight search tasks
All three models have 100% identical speed and reasoning capability, differing only in name
`sonnet` can only read image files, while `opus` can only read audio files
subagents-29.explanation: According to 'Choosing a Model and Color' in Chapter 2: Haiku is optimized for fast, lightweight tasks; Sonnet balances speed and depth well; Opus is strongest for complex analysis.

subagents-30.question: If a Subagent's `model` field is set to `inherit` (or omitted from the YAML Frontmatter), which model will that Subagent run on?
options: It will automatically use whatever model your main conversation is currently running
It will throw a `ModelNotFoundError` and refuse to launch
It will always force a downgrade to the oldest model from 2021
It will randomly run a different model on every line of code
subagents-30.explanation: `inherit` means inheritance: the subagent uses the exact same model that the main session is using. If you omit the `model:` line in YAML, it also defaults to `inherit`.

subagents-31.question: What is the practical purpose of choosing a `color` field (e.g., `color: orange` or `color: cyan`) for a Subagent?
options: Displays an identifying color in the Terminal/UI so you can quickly tell which subagent is active, which is especially helpful when multiple subagents are running
Determines the OS CPU scheduling priority (red runs faster than blue)
Changes the background color of all source code files in the project
Requires `color: orange` for the subagent to be allowed to call the `Bash` tool
subagents-31.explanation: 'This shows up in the UI so you can quickly tell which subagent is active. It's a small detail, but it helps when you have multiple subagents running.'

subagents-32.question: What is the standard list of 5 configuration fields in the YAML Frontmatter block of a `.claude/agents/<name>.md` file introduced in Chapter 2?
options: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`, and `color`
`id`, `password`, `port`, `host`, and `protocol`
`author`, `version`, `license`, `repository`, and `keywords`
`temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `stop_sequences`, and `stream`
subagents-32.explanation: The YAML Frontmatter block of a subagent configuration file consists of 5 basic fields: `name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`, and `color`.

subagents-33.question: What role does the `name` field in a Subagent's YAML Frontmatter play?
options: It is the unique identifier of the subagent, and also the name you use when asking Claude to invoke that specific subagent in a message
It is the password to unlock the configuration file
