claude-code-101-39.question: Why is the stage right after Claude presents its plan in `Plan Mode` called `the best place to course-correct`?
options: Because it's before any code is written — you can easily review the approach, change direction, or request edits to specific parts at the lowest possible cost
Because once code is written, your keyboard is locked and cannot be edited anymore
Because in Plan Mode you consume zero tokens
Because Git does not allow editing files after creating a new file
claude-code-101-39.explanation: According to Lesson 3.1: 'This is the best place to course-correct, because it's before any code is written.' Fixing a line in a plan is many times faster and cheaper than having Claude mistakenly edit 20 files and then untangling them.

claude-code-101-40.question: In the `Code` step (after the plan has been approved), what is the single most important factor for improving the quality of Claude's output before it considers the task finished?
options: Ensuring Claude can verify its own work before considering the task finished
Forbidding Claude from running any tests or checking tools
Setting a time limit forcing Claude to finish writing every feature within 3 seconds
Disabling all compiler error messages
claude-code-101-40.explanation: According to the 'Code' section (Lesson 3.1): 'Claude works best when it can verify its own work before considering the task finished, instead of you having to be the QA. Verification gives Claude a feedback loop — it runs tests or checks, sees the output, which helps inform Claude's next decisions.'

claude-code-101-41.question: What two practical tips does Lesson 3.1 recommend to make Claude's self-verification (`Verification`) during the `Code` phase more effective?
options: 1) Call out existing verification tools in the project (such as test suite commands or build scripts), and 2) Add new ways for Claude to check its work back and forth (such as installing the `Claude in Chrome extension` when building websites so Claude can open a tab and test the UI directly)
1) Delete the entire `tests/` directory of the project, and 2) Uninstall the Chrome browser
1) Always test manually by eye without letting Claude run commands, and 2) Close the Terminal
1) Only use the `echo` command to test, and 2) Never use `CLAUDE.md`
claude-code-101-41.explanation: Lesson 3.1 states 2 clear tips: (1) 'Call out existing verification tools' (telling Claude the existing test/linter commands), and (2) 'Add new ways for Claude to keep iterating and checking its work back and forth. For example, if you're building websites, install the Claude in Chrome extension so Claude Code can open a new browser tab and test the UI directly.'

claude-code-101-42.question: According to the `Quick tip` at the end of the `Code` section (Lesson 3.1), if you find Claude keeps running into the same issue repeatedly (e.g., how to run a tricky command or a project-specific convention), what should you do?
options: Ask Claude to write the solution/rule to its `CLAUDE.md` file so it remembers for all future sessions
Write the solution on a sticky note and stick it to your computer monitor
Delete the project and recreate it from scratch
Switch to a different programming language
claude-code-101-42.explanation: 'Quick tip: If you find Claude keeps running into the same issue, ask it to write the solution to its CLAUDE.md file.'

claude-code-101-43.question: In step 4 (`Commit`) of the `Explore -> Plan -> Code -> Commit` workflow, why should you do a quick check of the modified files (`git status` / `git diff`) before having Claude commit?
options: To make sure the commit is a clean point-in-time step on the codebase — free of leftover experimental code or scratch files that you and Claude might have tried along the way
Because Git requires the user to manually open every file before allowing `git commit`
Because Claude Code cannot run `git commit` or write commit messages
To delete all modified files before creating an empty commit
claude-code-101-43.explanation: According to the 'Commit' section (Lesson 3.1): 'Before you commit, do a quick check of the modified files to make sure the update is a clean point-in-time step on the codebase — it doesn't carry detritus that you and Claude might have tried on the way. Then get Claude to generate a commit message in your style, commit and push.'

claude-code-101-44.question: In the `Recap` of Lesson 3.1, how is the role of each step in the 4-step workflow `Explore, Plan, Code, and Commit` summarized?
options: `Explore` gives Claude relevant context; `Plan` creates a plan of action for you to review and course-correct; `Code` is the back-and-forth execution and verification; `Commit` helps you review and push clean code so you can start your next step cleanly
`Explore` is for deleting code; `Plan` is for pushing to Git; `Code` is for reading docs; `Commit` is for installing libraries
All 4 steps do the exact same thing: running `/clear`
`Explore` and `Plan` are only for beginners, while senior developers only need the `Commit` step
claude-code-101-44.explanation: The Lesson 3.1 Recap summarizes it clearly: Explore gives Claude the relevant context; Plan creates a plan of action that you can review and course-correct; Code is the back-and-forth between you and Claude before settling on the final solution; Commit helps you review and push your code so you can start on your next step cleanly.

claude-code-101-45.question: In Lesson 3.2 (`Context Management`), what is the potential risk of letting the Context Window fill up automatically and relying entirely on Claude Code's `Auto-compaction`?
options: When auto-compacting, Claude has to guess what is important to your task to keep — and it can potentially lose important details
When the Context Window fills up, Claude Code automatically charges 50x more per character
Auto-compaction wipes your `CLAUDE.md` file from your hard drive
Claude Code has no auto-compaction mechanism and will freeze your machine immediately
claude-code-101-45.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2 ('What Happens When Context Fills Up'): 'When you approach the limit, Claude Code automatically compacts your conversation so you can keep working. Most of the time this works fine, but Claude has to guess what's important to your task — and it can potentially lose details.'

claude-code-101-46.question: What does the `/compact` command in Claude Code do?
options: Compacts the conversation up to that point: freeing up Context Window space while KEEPING a summary of what you have already worked on
Wipes 100% of the conversation without keeping any summary
Compresses the entire project source folder into a `.zip` file
Displays the list of currently connected MCP servers
claude-code-101-46.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2 ('Commands'): 'You can trigger compaction yourself with the `/compact` command. This compacts everything up to that point. It's handy when you want to free up context space while keeping a summary of what you've already worked on.'

claude-code-101-47.question: What additional information can you pass along with the `/compact` command (for example: `/compact focus on the authentication API changes and database schema`)?
options: You can pass specific instructions telling Claude exactly what information is important to prioritize keeping in the summary during compaction
You can only pass an integer from 1 to 9
You are not allowed to pass any text after `/compact`, or it will throw a syntax error
You pass your GitHub account password to automatically push code
claude-code-101-47.explanation: Unlike auto-compaction (where Claude has to guess what matters), when you proactively run `/compact <instructions>`, you can tell Claude exactly which focus areas to preserve for the next step!

claude-code-101-48.question: How does the `/clear` command in Claude Code differ from `/compact`?
options: `/clear` wipes 100% of the current conversation context (`clears everything`) to start completely fresh with NO summary of the previous session
`/clear` keeps the entire chat history, whereas `/compact` wipes everything
`/clear` deletes all source code files in the project folder on your hard drive
`/clear` and `/compact` behave 100% identically
claude-code-101-48.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'If you want to start completely fresh, with no summary of the previous session, use `/clear`. This clears everything.'

claude-code-101-49.question: Which command do you use to check what is currently taking up space inside your Context Window along with a `visual graph`?
options: `/context`
`/compact`
`/clear`
`/init`
claude-code-101-49.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'To see what's actually in your context, run the `/context` command. You'll get a high-level overview of your context usage, what's taking up the most space, and a visual graph showing the breakdown.'

claude-code-101-50.question: According to the rule of thumb (`When to Use Which`) in Lesson 3.2, when should you use `/compact` and when should you use `/clear`?
options: Use `/compact` when you are STILL working on the same task and running up against the context limit; use `/clear` when you are SWITCHING to something unrelated (`CLAUDE.md` and `git history` are still there to give Claude the basics)
Use `/clear` when you are in the middle of a feature and need to remember the previous step; use `/compact` when switching to a different project
Always run both `/compact` and `/clear` together after every question
Never use `/clear` because it will delete your `CLAUDE.md` file
claude-code-101-50.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2 ('When to Use Which'): Use `/compact` when 'you're working on the same task and running up against the context limit'; use `/clear` when 'you're switching to something unrelated and don't want the previous context to confuse Claude. Your CLAUDE.md file and git history are still there to give Claude the basics.'

claude-code-101-51.question: According to `Tips for Saving Context Space` (Lesson 3.2), why should you keep your `CLAUDE.md` file concise?
options: Because `CLAUDE.md` gets loaded automatically into EVERY session; if it is bloated, it eats into your Context Window working space before you even start
Because Claude Code can only read up to the first 10 lines of `CLAUDE.md`
Because if `CLAUDE.md` is longer than 500 words, Git will refuse to commit
Because the longer `CLAUDE.md` is, the dimmer the text color becomes in the Terminal
claude-code-101-51.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'Be concise in your CLAUDE.md. That file gets loaded into every session, so if it's bloated, it's eating into your working space before you even start. Move detailed guidance that's only relevant sometimes into a skill or a separate file that you reference as needed.'

claude-code-101-52.question: Why do connected `MCP servers` consume Context Window space even when you do not invoke any of their tools in the conversation?
options: Because by default, every connected MCP server loads its tool definitions and schemas into your Context Window; therefore, you should use `/mcp` to disable servers you do not actively need
Because MCP servers automatically download video ads into the Terminal window
Because MCP servers duplicate your entire chat history every minute
MCP servers do not consume any tokens in the Context Window at all
claude-code-101-52.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'Manage your MCP servers. By default, connected MCP servers load their tool definitions into your context window, and should only stay enabled when you actually need them. Each server adds context overhead, so if you have servers configured for one project that you don't need in another, disable them with `/mcp`.'

claude-code-101-53.question: What is the 3rd tip for saving Context Window space in Lesson 3.2 when you need Claude to investigate a big question about your codebase without cluttering your main session?
options: Use subagents — tell Claude to delegate the investigation to a subagent so it works in its own context window and returns only a summary to your main thread
Run `/clear` after every single file Claude reads
Open the source files in a web browser and search manually by eye
Delete all `CLAUDE.md` and `.mcp.json` files
claude-code-101-53.explanation: According to Lesson 3.2: 'Use subagents. If you want to ask a big question about your codebase, but don't want the exploration to clutter up your main session, tell Claude to "use a subagent to investigate..." The subagent does the digging in its own context window and returns just a summary to your main agent, keeping your main context clean.'

claude-code-101-54.question: According to Lesson 3.3 (`Code Review`), what is the first and most natural step to review code when working with Claude Code?
options: Read through the work as it goes — watch the changes and ask questions or steer Claude right away if something looks off
Blindly click Approve on everything and push straight to Production without reading a single line
Wait until customers report a system crash before opening the code to inspect it
Print out the entire source code on paper once a month
claude-code-101-54.explanation: According to Lesson 3.3 ('Read through the work as it goes'): You remain ultimately responsible for what goes into the codebase. Reviewing diffs and asking questions while Claude works helps catch mistakes earliest.

claude-code-101-55.question: Why does Lesson 3.3 advise you NOT to only ask Claude to review code inside the SAME conversation session where it just wrote that code?
options: Because in that same session, Claude still carries all the context and reasoning justifying the decisions it just made (confirmation bias), making it more likely to overlook its own mistakes than a fresh, independent session!
Because Claude Code forbids users from typing the word `review` in a session that already has code
Because reviewing in the same session will automatically delete all newly written files
Because a single conversation session only allows sending at most 2 messages
claude-code-101-55.explanation: According to Lesson 3.3 ('Ask for a second opinion'): When reviewing in the same session where it wrote the code, the model already has the reasoning chain of why it wrote it that way, making it harder to spot blind spots. Using a fresh context yields a much more objective evaluation.

claude-code-101-56.question: How do you `Ask for a second opinion` with a completely fresh, objective context in Claude Code according to Lesson 3.3?
options: Run the built-in `/review` (or `/code-review`) command, or open a new Claude Code tab/session (or use an independent `code-reviewer` subagent) to inspect the changes without being influenced by the prior coding conversation
You must buy a second Anthropic account on a different computer
Run `/compact` and then ask Claude if it likes the code it just wrote
Switch the Terminal theme from dark mode to light mode
claude-code-101-56.explanation: The `/review` command (or opening a new session / invoking a review subagent) starts a clean context focused solely on reading the actual diff and source code, unbiased by the earlier coding discussion and without modifying your files.

claude-code-101-57.question: When a Code Review report returns a list of findings, how should you handle them according to `Decide what to do with each finding` (Lesson 3.3)?
options: Evaluate each item and decide: have Claude fix the genuinely important issues right away; create Issues for out-of-scope items to handle later; and ignore false positives or overly pedantic suggestions
You must have Claude fix 100% of every suggestion regardless of how trivial or inaccurate it is
Delete the entire review report without reading any item
Always refuse to fix any bugs found
claude-code-101-57.explanation: Not every comment from an AI reviewer needs immediate fixing: you decide which items to fix now (bugs, security, edge cases), which to defer to a later PR, and which are false positives you can safely skip.

claude-code-101-58.question: In `Check if parts of the codebase were missed` (Lesson 3.3), what common mistake occurs when making changes in a large project, and what should you ask Claude to prevent it?
options: Changes are applied in one place while other related files (callers, tests, types, docs) are forgotten; proactively ask Claude if any other parts of the codebase are affected by this change and still need updating
Claude automatically translates folder names into Spanish
Git automatically deletes old branches on the remote server
The browser automatically clears its browsing history
claude-code-101-58.explanation: When editing code, it is easy to update the core logic while forgetting to update callers, unit tests, or related documentation. Asking Claude to scan all related parts ensures consistency.

claude-code-101-59.question: According to `Try it out after fixing findings` (Lesson 3.3), why must you re-run tests and verify the application again after having Claude fix issues found during Code Review before committing?
options: Because the new fixes applied during review can themselves accidentally introduce new bugs (regressions); re-running tests and verifying ensures everything actually works smoothly before committing
Because Git does not allow running `git commit` unless Chrome is open
Because every code edit erases the contents of `CLAUDE.md`
Because Claude Code requires running at least 100 terminal commands before exiting
claude-code-101-59.explanation: Any code change — even one meant to fix a bug flagged during code review — carries the risk of introducing regressions. Always re-run tests/builds and verify in practice before committing!

claude-code-101-60.question: When using the `Claude in Chrome extension` together with Claude Code during Web application development (Lesson 3.1), what is the biggest benefit?
options: Claude Code can open a new browser tab, directly test the UI it just wrote, observe the results/console errors, and iterate on fixes until the UI works properly
It is only used to block ads when watching YouTube videos
It makes Chrome use 90% less RAM
It completely replaces the need for Git in the project
claude-code-101-60.explanation: According to Lesson 3.1: '...if you're building websites, install the Claude in Chrome extension so Claude Code can open a new browser tab and test the UI directly.' This creates a closed-loop verification feedback cycle for Frontend UI as well.

claude-code-101-61.question: If you have a very detailed workflow guide (hundreds of lines long) that is ONLY occasionally needed for a specialized task, where does Lesson 3.2 recommend placing it to avoid wasting Context Window space?
options: Move the detailed guidance into a `Skill` (or a separate documentation file referenced only when needed), keeping `CLAUDE.md` concise
Paste all hundreds of lines right at the top of `CLAUDE.md`
Duplicate that content into every source file in the project
Put it inside the name of an MCP Server
claude-code-101-61.explanation: 'Move detailed guidance that's only relevant sometimes into a skill or a separate file that you reference as needed.' This keeps normal sessions from wasting context unnecessarily.

claude-code-101-62.question: Suppose you just finished fixing a bug in the Payment system, committed everything cleanly, and now want to switch to building a completely new feature in the User Profile UI. Which command should you run in Claude Code before starting the new feature?
options: `/clear` (to wipe all context from the old Payment task, preventing it from confusing Claude on the new User Profile task)
`/compact` (to keep all details of the Payment system mixed into the new task)
`/context` (because this command automatically writes the new feature code)
`/mcp` (to delete all Git history)

claude-code-101-63.question: Suppose you are midway through a 5-stage Authentication system refactoring, you just finished stage 2, and you see the Context Window is 85% full. Which command should you run to continue to stage 3?
options: `/compact` (to free up Context Window space while keeping a summary of what was done in stages 1 and 2)
`/clear` (to wipe all memory of stages 1 and 2)
`exit` and uninstall Claude Code
`git reset --hard` to delete all newly written code

claude-code-101-64.question: When you run `/context` in Claude Code, what useful information is displayed on screen?
options: An overview of current Context Window usage, a breakdown of what is taking up the most space (System prompt, MCP tools, Memory files, Messages, etc.), and a visual graph of the allocation
A list of Wi-Fi passwords for all nearby networks
A graph of CPU temperature and hard drive spin speed
The entire commit history of every repository on GitHub
claude-code-101-64.explanation: `/context` gives a transparent view of where your working memory (Context Window) is being spent, making it easy to spot if an MCP server or `CLAUDE.md` file is taking up too much space.

claude-code-101-65.question: According to the `Recap` of Lesson 3.3 (`Code Review`), what are the 3 core steps for performing an effective Code Review with Claude's help?
options: 1) Read through the changes yourself and run `/review` (or a new session) for a second opinion in a clean context, 2) Decide which findings are actually worth fixing and check for missed parts, 3) Re-test the application after fixing issues before committing
1) Have Claude self-review in the same coding session, 2) Accept every suggestion without reading, 3) Commit immediately without re-running tests

claude-code-101-66.question: What role does the `CLAUDE.md` file play in Claude Code, and when is it loaded?
options: It provides persistent memory about your project; Claude Code reads it automatically every time you start a new session and appends its contents to your prompt
It is read only once when you install your operating system and deleted immediately afterward
It stores the project's compiled binary code and is only loaded when you type `/mcp`
It is a log file strictly for human readers; Claude Code completely ignores it

It gives Claude Code persistent memory about your project... Claude Code reads it automatically every time you start a session. CLAUDE.md files are appended to your prompt.'

claude-code-101-67.question: If a project does NOT have a `CLAUDE.md` file, what limitation occurs every time you start a new Claude Code session?

Claude Code refuses to launch and throws `MissingClaudeMdException`
Claude Code automatically deletes all files in the project directory
You will not be able to use the `Shift + Tab` shortcut

Sometimes it makes assumptions, which makes it harder to steer back in the right direction.'

claude-code-101-68.question: In the typical example in Lesson 4.1 (`An Example`), what 3 main groups of information does a clean, effective `CLAUDE.md` file usually include?

claude-code-101-69.question: According to `CLAUDE.md is for Teams` (Lesson 4.1), what is the difference between `Project-level CLAUDE.md` and `User-level CLAUDE.md`?

`Project-level CLAUDE.md` only works on Windows, while `User-level CLAUDE.md` only works on macOS
You are only allowed to use one of the two files; the system never combines both
`User-level CLAUDE.md` must be pushed to the company's public GitHub repository

claude-code-101-70.question: According to `Tips` in Lesson 4.1, if you find yourself repeatedly correcting Claude on the same thing (e.g., always reminding it to use Server Actions instead of API routes), what is the fastest way to save that rule to memory?

Close Claude Code, uninstall it, and reinstall it from scratch
Run `/clear` 5 times in a row
Switch the permission mode to `Plan Mode`

claude-code-101-71.question: How can you reference an existing documentation file in your project (such as `README.md` or `docs/api.md`) from inside `CLAUDE.md` so Claude knows to read it when needed?

claude-code-101-72.question: Why does Lesson 4.1 recommend `Start without one` (starting a project without creating `CLAUDE.md` from minute one, and running `/init` later)?

Because `/init` only works after a project has at least 1,000 Git commits
Because if you create `CLAUDE.md` at the start, Claude Code cannot read source files
Because `CLAUDE.md` automatically expires after 24 hours
claude-code-101-72.explanation: According to Lesson 4.1: 'Start without one. We recommend starting a project without a CLAUDE.md file so you can see where you constantly have to course-correct the model. This keeps your CLAUDE.md compact and focused on only the necessary information. When you're ready, run `/init` to have Claude generate one for you.'

claude-code-101-73.question: In Lesson 4.2 (`Subagents`), if you create or add a new Subagent configuration file to `.claude/agents/` while a Claude Code session is already open, what must you do for Claude Code to load that new Subagent?

Change the file extension from `.md` to `.json`

claude-code-101-74.question: According to `Further Customization` in Lesson 4.2 (`Subagents`), when you preload Skills into a Subagent by adding the `skills` key to its YAML frontmatter, how does this loading mechanism differ from how Skills work in the main conversation?

In a Subagent, only the Skill's name is loaded while the body of the Skill is completely stripped
Skills declared in a Subagent are automatically disabled and cannot be used
There is no difference between the two mechanisms

claude-code-101-75.question: Besides preloading Skills (`skills` key), what other advanced Subagent customization feature mentioned in `Further Customization` (Lesson 4.2) helps a Subagent work more effectively when used repeatedly on the same project?

`Global broadcasting` — lets the subagent send messages to every computer on the LAN
`Infinite recursion` — lets the subagent call itself infinitely

claude-code-101-76.question: In Lesson 4.3 (`Skills`), what is the core difference between placing instructions in `CLAUDE.md` versus placing them in a `Skill` (`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`)?
options: `CLAUDE.md` is always loaded in full into EVERY session (for always-needed info), whereas `Skills` only load `name` and `description` initially and load the full `SKILL.md` content on-demand when a task matches or when you type `/skill-name`
`Skills` are always loaded 100% into every session, whereas `CLAUDE.md` is only loaded when you run `/claude-md`
`CLAUDE.md` can only be written in English, whereas `Skills` can only be written in Python
`Skills` cannot be shared via Git; only `CLAUDE.md` can be shared via Git

claude-code-101-77.question: How do you trigger a Skill in Claude Code?
options: Either let Claude automatically invoke it when your request matches the Skill's `description`, or manually type `/<skill-name>` (slash command) directly in the chat

claude-code-101-78.question: If you create a Skill (e.g., a `release-notes` workflow or a sensitive script) and ONLY want it to run when you manually type `/<skill-name>` — preventing Claude from invoking it automatically — which setting should you add to the YAML frontmatter of `SKILL.md`?

claude-code-101-79.question: According to Lesson 4.4 (`MCP`), what problem does the `Model Context Protocol (MCP)` solve for Claude Code?

It is a file compression algorithm that shrinks hard drive usage by 10x
It is a color theme engine for changing VS Code's background
It is a compiler that translates Python code into Java

A lot of your context lives outside your codebase — in databases, productivity apps, or public repositories. MCP bridges that gap.'

claude-code-101-80.question: In Lesson 4.4, what two real-world examples are given to illustrate what you can do when connecting an MCP Server to Claude Code?

If you need up-to-date documentation for a specific coding task, an MCP server like Context7 can provide that to Claude Code.'

claude-code-101-81.question: Which CLI command do you use to add a new MCP Server to Claude Code, and what are the two server connection types introduced in Lesson 4.4?
options: Use `claude mcp add`, with 2 server types: 1) `HTTP servers` (for remote services connected over the network), and 2) `Stdio servers` (for local processes running directly on your machine)

There are two types: HTTP servers are for remote services (hosted by the service provider and connect over the network); Stdio servers are for local processes that run on your machine.'

claude-code-101-82.question: Inside a Claude Code session, which command do you run to see which MCP servers are connected, check for connection errors, and disable servers you do not need?
options: `/mcp`
`/hooks`
`/agents`
`/compact`
claude-code-101-82.explanation: According to Lesson 4.4: 'You can manage your servers with `/mcp` inside a Claude Code session to see what's connected, check errors, and disable servers you don't need.'

claude-code-101-83.question: According to `Scoping Servers` (Lesson 4.4), what are the 3 levels at which MCP servers in Claude Code can be scoped?
options: 1) `Local` (only enabled in the current project, just for you), 2) `User` (available across all your projects), and 3) `Project` (uses a `.mcp.json` file checked into Git so everyone on the team shares the same servers)
1) `Frontend`, 2) `Backend`, and 3) `Database`
1) `Development`, 2) `Staging`, and 3) `Production`
1) `Read-only`, 2) `Auto-accept`, and 3) `Plan`
claude-code-101-83.explanation: According to 'Scoping Servers' (Lesson 4.4): (1) Local — only enabled in the current project, just for you; (2) User — available across all your projects; (3) Project — uses a `.mcp.json` file that you check into version control so everyone on the team gets the same servers.

claude-code-101-84.question: When you configure an MCP server at the `Project` scope to share with all team members via Git, which file stores that MCP server configuration?
options: `.mcp.json`
`CLAUDE.md`
`package-lock.json`
`.gitignore`
claude-code-101-84.explanation: According to Lesson 4.4: 'Project — uses a `.mcp.json` file that you check into version control so everyone on the team gets the same servers.'

claude-code-101-85.question: According to `Context Costs` (Lesson 4.4), why is having too many MCP servers connected simultaneously detrimental to your Context Window?
options: Because MCP servers always load all of their `tool names and schemas` into your Context Window even when you are not actively using them in that session
Because each MCP server automatically deletes 1,000 lines of code in your project
Because MCP servers force Claude Code to disable Auto-compaction
Because MCP servers corrupt the formatting of `CLAUDE.md`
claude-code-101-85.explanation: According to Lesson 4.4 ('Context Costs'): 'MCP servers add their tool names and schemas into your context window, even when you're not actively using them. Each connected server takes up space, so run `/mcp` to see what's connected and disable anything you're not actively using.'

claude-code-101-86.question: According to Lesson 4.5 (`Hooks`), what is `The big difference` between `Hooks` and everything else covered in Claude Code 101 (`CLAUDE.md`, `Skills`, `Subagents`, `MCP`)?
options: Hooks are DETERMINISTIC — they always run 100% of the time without exception, turning your rules into absolute guarantees rather than mere suggestions to the AI model!
Hooks only run when the AI model feels like it, whereas `CLAUDE.md` is 100% deterministic
Hooks are the only feature used to chat with the user by voice
Hooks only work on the Web interface and not in the Terminal
claude-code-101-86.explanation: The opening of Lesson 4.5 states: 'Hooks let you run commands at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle. The big difference between hooks and everything else covered in this course is that hooks are deterministic — they always run.'

claude-code-101-87.question: Why should you use a `Hook` to run a code formatter (like `Prettier` or `gofmt`) after every file edit instead of just writing `'Run Prettier after every file edit'` in `CLAUDE.md`?
options: Because when written in `CLAUDE.md`, Claude will follow it most of the time but sometimes it won't; whereas a Hook guarantees Prettier executes 100% of the time with no exceptions!
Because `CLAUDE.md` does not allow mentioning the tool name `Prettier`
Because running Prettier via a Hook does not require Node.js to be installed on the machine
Because a Hook runs slower than `CLAUDE.md` but looks prettier
claude-code-101-87.explanation: According to Lesson 4.5 ('Why Use Hooks'): 'You can tell Claude in your CLAUDE.md to run Prettier after every file edit. Most of the time it will. But sometimes it won't. A hook makes it happen every single time, no exceptions... Hooks turn your team's conventions into guarantees, not suggestions.'

claude-code-101-88.question: Where are Hooks in Claude Code configured, and what are the 5 common `lifecycle events` listed in Lesson 4.5?
options: Configured in `settings.json` (such as `.claude/settings.json`), with the 5 common events being: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, and `Notification`
Configured in `.mcp.json`, with the 5 events being: `OnClick`, `OnHover`, `OnScroll`, `OnLoad`, and `OnResize`
Configured in `CLAUDE.md`, with the 5 events being: `GitInit`, `GitAdd`, `GitCommit`, `GitPush`, and `GitPull`
Configured in `package.json`, with the 5 events being: `Start`, `Pause`, `Resume`, `Kill`, and `Restart`
claude-code-101-88.explanation: According to 'How They Work' (Lesson 4.5): Hooks are configured in `settings.json` with common events including: `PreToolUse` (before a tool call), `PostToolUse` (after a tool finishes), `UserPromptSubmit` (when the user submits a prompt), `Stop` (when Claude finishes responding), and `Notification` (when Claude sends a notification).

claude-code-101-89.question: Inside a Claude Code session, which command can you run to open a read-only list to verify whether your configured Hooks are showing up properly?
options: `/hooks`
`/mcp`
`/context`
`/review`
claude-code-101-89.explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: Running `/hooks` inside Claude Code opens a read-only list of your configured hooks, so you can check that new ones show up.

claude-code-101-90.question: To set up the most common Hook — auto-formatting code right after every time Claude edits or creates a file — which event should you choose and what should the `matcher` field be set to?
options: Choose the `PostToolUse` event with a `matcher` of `"Edit|Write"`
Choose the `PreToolUse` event with a `matcher` of `"Read|Grep"`
Choose the `UserPromptSubmit` event with a `matcher` of `"Bash"`
Choose the `Notification` event with no `matcher`
claude-code-101-90.explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: 'The most common hook is auto-formatting after edits. Set a `PostToolUse` hook with a matcher of `"Edit|Write"` so it fires after Claude uses the Edit or Write tool. The command checks the file extension and runs the appropriate formatter.'

claude-code-101-91.question: When a Hook attached to the `PreToolUse` event is triggered, how does it receive information about the `tool name` and `input` arguments Claude is about to call?
options: The Hook receives the tool name and input as JSON on standard input `stdin`
The Hook must read from a screenshot image file on the hard drive
The Hook receives information through the microphone audio port
`PreToolUse` has no way of knowing which tool or arguments Claude is about to call
claude-code-101-91.explanation: According to 'Blocking with PreToolUse' (Lesson 4.5): 'PreToolUse hooks can block tool calls before they happen. Your hook receives the tool name and input as JSON on stdin. The exit code determines what happens.'

claude-code-101-92.question: In a `PreToolUse` Hook, if your validation script wants to BLOCK Claude's tool call and send the rejection reason back to Claude so it can adjust, what `Exit code` must your script return and where must it print the message?
options: Return `Exit code 2` and write the blocking reason to standard error `stderr` (which gets fed back to Claude as feedback so it knows why it was blocked and can adjust)
Return `Exit code 0` and print nothing
Return `Exit code 1` and write the message into `README.md`
Return `Exit code 404` and power off the computer
claude-code-101-92.explanation:
This is a critical concept in Lesson 4.5 ('Blocking with PreToolUse'):
- `Exit code 0` — proceed normally.
- `Exit code 2` — block the action. The stderr message gets fed back to Claude as feedback so it knows why it was blocked and can adjust.
- `Any other exit code` — a non-blocking error that gets shown to you but doesn't stop anything.

claude-code-101-93.question: What happens if a `PreToolUse` Hook returns `Exit code 1` (or any exit code other than `0` and `2`)?
options: It is treated as a `non-blocking error`: the error message is shown to the user, but it does NOT stop Claude's tool call!
It blocks the action identically to `Exit code 2`
It deletes the project's `settings.json` file
It automatically switches Claude Code into `Plan Mode`
claude-code-101-93.explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: Only `Exit code 2` actually blocks a tool call. Any exit code other than `0` and `2` (such as `Exit code 1`) is simply 'a non-blocking error that gets shown to you but doesn't stop anything'.

claude-code-101-94.question: To share your Hooks configuration with all team members via a Git repository (`Sharing Hooks with Your Team`), which file should you place the Hooks configuration in and which environment variable should you use when referencing scripts stored in the project?
options: Place the configuration in `.claude/settings.json` (committed to the repo) and use the `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` environment variable in commands to reference project scripts (ensuring they work regardless of Claude's current working directory)
Place the configuration in `/tmp/settings.json` and use an absolute path containing your personal username like `C:\Users\kuga\...`
Place the configuration in `.gitignore` so nobody can see it
Place the configuration in the `$HOME_PASSWORD` environment variable
claude-code-101-94.explanation: According to the end of Lesson 4.5 ('Sharing Hooks with Your Team'): 'Hooks configured in `.claude/settings.json` are project-level and can be checked into your repo... Use the `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` environment variable in your commands to reference scripts stored in your project, so they work regardless of Claude's current working directory.'

claude-code-101-95.question: Which Hook event in `settings.json` fires right when you press Enter to submit a prompt, BEFORE Claude begins processing it?
options: `UserPromptSubmit`
`PostToolUse`
`Stop`
`Notification`
claude-code-101-95.explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: '`UserPromptSubmit` — runs when you submit a prompt, before Claude processes it.'

claude-code-101-96.question: Which Hook event runs right when Claude finishes responding for a turn?
options: `Stop`
`PreToolUse`
`UserPromptSubmit`
`PostToolUse`
claude-code-101-96.explanation: According to Lesson 4.5: '`Stop` — runs when Claude finishes responding' (very useful for running end-of-turn checks or playing a sound/notification when a long task completes).

options: (1) `CLAUDE.md` • (2) `Hooks` • (3) `MCP` • (4) `Skills` • (5) `Subagents`
(1) `Hooks` • (2) `MCP` • (3) `CLAUDE.md` • (4) `Subagents` • (5) `Skills`

claude-code-101-97.explanation: This summarizes all of Chapter 4: (1) `CLAUDE.md` for project memory always loaded each session; (2) `Hooks` for 100% deterministic actions like auto-formatting; (3) `MCP` to connect external services like Linear/Context7; (4) `Skills` for specialized workflows loaded on demand; and (5) `Subagents` to isolate context-heavy tasks.

claude-code-101-98.question: When collaborating as a team on a Git repository, which Claude Code configuration files and directories should be committed to version control so the whole team benefits?

Your personal `~/.claude/` directory on your local hard drive and `.env` files containing secret keys
No Claude Code files are ever allowed to be committed to Git
The entire `node_modules/` and `.venv/` directories

claude-code-101-99.question: In Lab 04 (`customizing_claude_code.py`), when `evaluate_pre_tool_use_exit_code(2, 'Direct editing of the .env file is not allowed!')` is called, what does the return value indicate?

The action is still allowed to run normally (`blocked: False`)
The error message is only shown to the user, and Claude receives no feedback
The entire session is wiped just like running `/clear`

Always skip planning -> Never verify AI-generated code -> Stuff everything into a 50,000-line `CLAUDE.md` file -> Enable all unused MCP servers
Only use Claude Code for theoretical Q&A without letting it read files or run terminal commands
Always review code in the same session where it was written and never re-run unit tests after fixing bugs
claude-code-101-100.explanation: This answer encapsulates all 4 chapters (12 lessons) of the official *Claude Code 101* course from Anthropic Academy!

agent-skills-1.question: In Claude Code, what is the exact definition of a 'Skill' (Agent Skill)?
options: A folder containing instructions and resources (centered around a `SKILL.md` file with `name` and `description` in its YAML frontmatter) that Claude Code can automatically discover and use on demand
A new large language model (LLM) retrained from scratch using your GPU
A system configuration file that can only run on Anthropic's cloud servers
A JavaScript snippet embedded into a browser to change the color theme of the Terminal
agent-skills-1.explanation: Skills are folders of instructions and resources that Claude Code can automatically discover and load on demand. Each skill lives in its own directory containing a `SKILL.md` file with `name` and `description` in the YAML frontmatter.

agent-skills-2.question: How does Claude Code decide when to activate a Skill for your request?
options: Claude matches your request against the `description` field in the YAML frontmatter of available skills and activates the relevant ones
Claude always activates all skills installed on your computer simultaneously for every prompt
Claude randomly picks a skill from the `.claude/skills/` directory
Claude only activates a skill when your code filename matches the skill name 100%
agent-skills-2.explanation: The `description` field in the YAML frontmatter is the core routing mechanism: when you ask Claude to do something, it semantically matches your request against the list of skill `description` values and automatically loads the appropriate skill.

agent-skills-3.question: What is a practical sign that you should write a new Skill in Claude Code?
options: When you notice yourself repeatedly explaining the same workflow, standard, or response structure to Claude across different conversations
When you only have a single one-off question that will never be repeated
When you want to change your Windows OS login password
When you want to increase your computer's physical hard drive capacity
agent-skills-3.explanation: The golden rule in Chapter 1: 'If you notice you're explaining the same thing to Claude repeatedly, that's a skill waiting to be written.' (For example: PR review standards, commit message formatting, or documentation standards).

agent-skills-4.question: What are the two minimum metadata fields in the YAML frontmatter block at the top of `SKILL.md` used to identify and trigger a skill?
options: `name` and `description`
`import` and `export`
`username` and `password`
`port` and `host`
agent-skills-4.explanation: Every `SKILL.md` file starts with YAML frontmatter (between two `---` lines) containing `name` (the skill's identifier) and `description` (which helps Claude know when to activate that skill).

agent-skills-5.question: On macOS and Linux, where are Personal Skills (personal skills that follow you across all projects) stored?
options: `~/.claude/skills/` (in the user's Home directory)
`/tmp/claude/skills/`
`/var/log/skills/`
`./node_modules/.skills/`
agent-skills-5.explanation: Personal skills reside at `~/.claude/skills/` (your home directory) and are automatically available across every project you work on on that machine.

agent-skills-6.question: On Windows, where is your Personal Skills directory located?
options: `C:\Users\<username>\.claude\skills`
`C:\Windows\System32\skills`
`C:\Program Files\Claude\skills`
`D:\Temp\skills`
agent-skills-6.explanation: On Windows, the Home directory `~` corresponds to `C:\Users\<username>`, so Personal skills are placed at `C:\Users\<username>\.claude\skills`.

agent-skills-7.question: Where are Project Skills (skills tied to a specific project and shared with the team via Git) stored?
options: In the `.claude/skills/` directory at the root directory of the project repository
In `~/.claude/skills/` on the team lead's personal machine
In the project's MySQL database table
In the `.git/hooks/` directory
agent-skills-7.explanation: Project skills reside at `.claude/skills/` inside the repository's root directory. When committed to version control (Git), any team member who clones the project automatically has these skills available.

agent-skills-8.question: Which of the following examples is best suited to be saved as a **Personal Skill** (`~/.claude/skills/`) rather than a Project Skill?
options: Your personal commit message style, private note formatting, or how you want Claude to explain code to you across all projects
Mandatory microservice architecture standards for the entire company team on a single product repo
Shared marketing department brand guidelines checks on a shared repo
Mandatory integration testing checklist before merging for the entire development team
agent-skills-8.explanation: Personal skills (`~/.claude/skills/`) are for personal preferences and workflows that follow you across different projects; shared team standards for a specific codebase belong in Project skills (`.claude/skills/`).

agent-skills-9.question: What is the most important difference between `CLAUDE.md` and `Skills` regarding when they are loaded into the Context Window?
options: `CLAUDE.md` is always loaded in full into EVERY conversation from the start, whereas `Skills` are only loaded on demand when your request matches their description
`Skills` are always loaded in full into every conversation, whereas `CLAUDE.md` is only loaded when you type `/claude`
Neither `CLAUDE.md` nor `Skills` ever consume any tokens in the Context Window
`CLAUDE.md` is only for Python, whereas `Skills` are only for JavaScript
agent-skills-9.explanation: `CLAUDE.md` loads into every conversation (always-on for foundational rules), while Skills load on demand (initially only `name` + `description` are loaded, and the full `SKILL.md` content is only loaded when relevant to save Context Window space).

agent-skills-10.question: Why should you NOT put a 400-line Pull Request review checklist directly into `CLAUDE.md`?
options: Because `CLAUDE.md` is loaded into every conversation; putting a PR review checklist there wastes Context Window tokens even when you are only debugging a bug or writing a new function
Because `CLAUDE.md` has a hard limit of at most 10 characters
Because Claude Code will throw a syntax error and refuse to start if `CLAUDE.md` contains bulleted lists
Because `CLAUDE.md` cannot be stored in a Git repository
agent-skills-10.explanation: A PR review checklist is only needed when you actually ask for a PR review. Putting it into a Skill (`.claude/skills/pr-review/SKILL.md`) ensures it is only loaded into context when you request a review, keeping normal debugging sessions lightweight.

agent-skills-11.question: What is the fundamental difference between **Skills** and traditional **Slash Commands**?
options: Slash Commands require the user to actively remember and type the command (e.g., `/review`) every time they want to run it, whereas Skills are automatically applied by Claude when it detects your request matches the context
Slash Commands run automatically without typing, whereas Skills require typing the full filename every time
Slash Commands cannot contain instruction text, whereas Skills can only contain 1 line of command
There is no difference whatsoever between these two concepts
agent-skills-11.explanation: With Slash Commands, the burden of remembering to invoke them falls on the user (you have to type `/...`). With Skills, Claude automatically recognizes the situation from your natural prompt and loads the matching skill (though every skill also supports invocation via `/skill-name` if you want).

agent-skills-12.question: When you open Claude Code and haven't sent any request related to a skill yet, what part of that skill does Claude load into the initial context?
options: Only the `name` and `description` (so Claude knows the catalog of available skills without filling up the Context Window)
100% of the `SKILL.md` file along with all files in `references/` and `scripts/`
Nothing at all, not even the skill name
Only the last 10 lines of the `SKILL.md` file
agent-skills-12.explanation: Initially, Claude only reads `name` and `description` from each skill's YAML frontmatter. This allows you to install dozens of skills while consuming almost no Context Window space.

agent-skills-13.question: Below the YAML frontmatter (closed by the second `---` line) in `SKILL.md`, what content do you write?
options: Detailed Markdown instructions (checklists, step-by-step workflows, output formatting rules, or whatever Claude needs to know to perform that task)
Compiled binary bytecode
The plain-text `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret key
Only HTML `<div>` and `<span>` tags are allowed
agent-skills-13.explanation: Below the YAML frontmatter is the standard Markdown body containing all the actual instructions for the task.

agent-skills-14.question: When a skill (e.g., `pr-review`) is automatically triggered by Claude in the Claude Code CLI, what does the user see on screen?
options: Claude displays a notification showing it invoked/loaded the skill (e.g., `Skill(pr-review)` -> `Successfully loaded skill`) before proceeding with the work according to the instructions
The Terminal window automatically closes and restarts the computer
Claude deletes all previous chat history
Claude operates completely silently without ever letting the user know which skill was loaded
agent-skills-14.explanation: As illustrated in the Chapter 1 lesson, when you ask 'Can you review the pull request on branch feat/auth?', Claude Code clearly displays `Skill(pr-review) -> Successfully loaded skill` before executing the review steps.

agent-skills-15.question: Which of the following scenarios is the MOST IDEAL candidate to package as an Agent Skill?
options: A fixed 5-step security audit and release notes writing workflow that your team performs weekly
A 1-line rule: 'This project uses Python 3.13 and uv for package management'
A single one-off lookup question: 'What is the capital of France?'
Automatically running the `eslint --fix` linter at the OS level every time a `.ts` file is saved to disk
agent-skills-15.explanation: A repeatable multi-step task workflow (such as generating release notes or performing a security audit) is the ideal use case for a Skill. A global 1-line rule belongs in `CLAUDE.md`, and automatic actions on file save belong in `Hooks`.

agent-skills-16.question: If a new colleague joins your team and clones the project repository, what do they need to do to use the Project Skills located in `.claude/skills/` of that repo?
options: Nothing extra — as soon as they open Claude Code in that project directory, the Project Skills in `.claude/skills/` are automatically discovered and ready to use
They must manually copy all those files to `C:\Windows`
They must pay a separate license fee for each `SKILL.md` file
They must compile `SKILL.md` into an `.exe` file before running
agent-skills-16.explanation: Project skills in `.claude/skills/` are committed to Git and are automatically discovered by Claude Code as soon as anyone clones the repo and opens Claude Code in that project directory.

agent-skills-17.question: In the YAML frontmatter block of `SKILL.md`, which character sequence is used on the opening and closing lines to delimit the frontmatter?
options: Three hyphens `---`
Three exclamation marks `!!!`
Three hash symbols `###`
`<yaml>` and `</yaml>` tags
agent-skills-17.explanation: Following standard Markdown YAML Frontmatter conventions, the metadata block at the top of `SKILL.md` must open with a `---` line and close with a `---` line.

agent-skills-18.question: Which statement is TRUE when comparing how a Skill is organized versus a typical standalone Markdown file?
options: Each Skill is a dedicated folder containing `SKILL.md`, and that folder can also include supporting resources such as scripts, reference documents (references), or templates (assets)
A Skill is only allowed to contain a single text file and strictly forbids any subdirectories inside
All of your Skills must be written together inside one single `SKILL.md` file
A Skill is not allowed to contain Markdown headings (`#`, `##`)
agent-skills-18.explanation: Right from the definition in Lesson 1: 'Skills are folders of instructions and resources'. Having each skill as its own directory (`<skill-name>/SKILL.md`) allows it to scale flexibly with attached scripts and reference documents.

agent-skills-19.question: When you have a foundational rule that you want Claude to ALWAYS remember in every conversation (e.g., 'Always use TypeScript instead of JavaScript'), where should you place it?
options: In the `CLAUDE.md` file
In a Skill named `random-skill` with no description
In the `.gitignore` file
In the `assets/` folder of a plugin
agent-skills-19.explanation: `CLAUDE.md` loads into every conversation, so global rules that must always be followed in every chat turn—like 'Always use TypeScript'—belong in `CLAUDE.md`.

agent-skills-20.question: In summary, what is the core benefit of using Agent Skills in Claude Code?
options: Packaging domain expertise and repeatable workflows once so Claude automatically applies them on demand at the right time, ensuring accurate work while keeping the Context Window lean
Making Claude run faster by completely disabling safety checks
Completely replacing the need for Git and version control systems
Allowing Claude Code to run without an internet connection or API
agent-skills-20.explanation: Agent Skills simultaneously solve workflow standardization (not having to re-explain things repeatedly) and context memory optimization (only loading on demand when the task matches).

agent-skills-21.question: When creating a new Project Skill named `accessibility-audit`, what is the exact file path and filename you need to create?
options: `.claude/skills/accessibility-audit/SKILL.md`
`.claude/skills/accessibility-audit.md`
`.claude/skills/accessibility-audit/skill.md`
`.claude/SKILL.md`
agent-skills-21.explanation: Each skill must reside in a subdirectory matching the skill name under `.claude/skills/`, and the configuration file must be named exactly `SKILL.md` (with SKILL in uppercase).

agent-skills-22.question: Why should the skill folder name (e.g., `.claude/skills/accessibility-audit/`) match the `name` field in the YAML frontmatter (`name: accessibility-audit`)?
options: To ensure consistent skill identification, create the `/accessibility-audit` command, and pass the Skills Validator check without an identifier mismatch error
Because the operating system does not allow creating Markdown files if the folder name differs from the first line of the file
Because Git will automatically delete the folder if the folder name does not match the `name` field
To encrypt `SKILL.md` using the AES-256 algorithm
agent-skills-22.explanation: The Agent Skills specification requires the directory name to match `name` in the frontmatter (lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens `-`) for consistent skill and slash command identification.

agent-skills-23.question: After creating a skill in Claude Code, what command can you type in the chat input to inspect the list of all currently loaded skills?
options: `/skills`
`/list-all-files`
`/show-markdown`
`/check-ram`
agent-skills-23.explanation: The `/skills` command (or asking Claude directly 'What skills do you have available?') lists all successfully loaded User skills, Project skills, and Plugin skills.

agent-skills-24.question: Besides asking a natural-language question for Claude to automatically trigger the `accessibility-audit` skill, how else can you explicitly invoke this skill?
options: Type the slash command corresponding to the skill name: `/accessibility-audit`
Press `Ctrl + Alt + Delete`
Type `import accessibility_audit` in the Terminal
Rename `SKILL.md` to `RUN.md`
agent-skills-24.explanation: When loaded into Claude Code, every skill automatically registers a slash command matching its name (`/skill-name`), allowing you to invoke it directly at any time.

agent-skills-25.question: How does the two-stage 'How Skill Matching Works' process in Claude Code operate?
options: Stage 1 (Startup): Scans and loads only `name` + `description` of all skills. Stage 2 (On-demand): When your request matches a `description`, Claude reads the full content of that `SKILL.md` file into the conversation
Stage 1: Reads 100% of all `SKILL.md` files at startup. Stage 2: Deletes unused skills after 5 minutes
Stage 1: Uploads the entire hard drive to the cloud. Stage 2: Downloads executable binaries
Stage 1: Runs all scripts in `scripts/`. Stage 2: Reads the YAML frontmatter

agent-skills-26.question: Suppose you create the `accessibility-audit` skill with super detailed instructions inside the `SKILL.md` body about WCAG, ARIA, and color contrast, but in the frontmatter you only write `description: Frontend helper`. agent-skills-27.question: When multiple skills across different scopes share the same name (e.g., all named `code-review`), what is the Priority Order from HIGHEST to LOWEST that Claude Code applies?
options: 1. Enterprise -> 2. Personal -> 3. Project -> 4. Plugins

1. Project -> 2. Personal -> 3. Plugins -> 4. Enterprise
1. Personal -> 2. Enterprise -> 3. Plugins -> 4. Project

agent-skills-28.question: Why is the **Enterprise** level designed to be at priority #1 (higher than both Personal and Project)?
options: So organizations/enterprises can enforce mandatory security, compliance, and company-wide workflow standards that no personal or project setting can accidentally or intentionally override
Because Enterprise files are always smaller in size than Personal files
Because Enterprise skills do not use Markdown format
Simply to sort alphabetically with E before P
agent-skills-28.explanation: Placing Enterprise at the highest priority ensures organizations can guarantee that mandatory company standards and security checks are always consistently enforced without being overridden by local configs.

agent-skills-29.question: A developer creates a Personal Skill at `~/.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md`. Later, they clone a team project that also has a Project Skill at `.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md`. When they ask for a code review in that project, what happens?
options: Their Personal Skill `code-review` will be used and will completely override/shadow the team's Project Skill `code-review`, because Personal has higher priority than Project!
The team's Project Skill will override their Personal Skill
Claude will merge the contents of both `SKILL.md` files into a single file
Claude will refuse to run both and report a duplicate name error

agent-skills-30.question: What is the best practice to avoid having your Personal Skills accidentally override your team's Project Skills?

Always name all skills with a random number
Move the entire contents of all skills into `.gitignore`

agent-skills-31.question: When you edit the contents of a `SKILL.md` file while a Claude Code session is open, do you have to exit and restart Claude Code?

agent-skills-32.question: If you just installed or updated a new **Plugin** containing skills while Claude Code is already open, which command lets you load the skills from that plugin immediately without restarting the session?

agent-skills-33.question: What principle does Claude's skill-matching mechanism rely on?

Prompt length matching: long questions trigger the skill with the longest file
File creation time matching: the most recently created `SKILL.md` file is always chosen

agent-skills-34.question: What is the standard naming convention for a skill's `name` field and its containing folder?

agent-skills-35.question: When testing a newly written skill, why does the lesson recommend testing with natural requests before using the `/skill-name` command?

agent-skills-36.question: In the Markdown body of `SKILL.md` for the `accessibility-audit` skill, what benefit does clearly specifying an `Output Format` section (e.g., grouping results into *Critical Violations*, *Warnings*, *Passed Checks*) provide?

Reduces the number of files in the project directory

agent-skills-37.question: Once a skill has been activated and `SKILL.md` has been loaded into the current conversation, you ask Claude a follow-up question related to the same task in the same chat session. What happens?

agent-skills-39.question: If a skill from a third-party **Plugin** has the same name as a **Project Skill** in your team's repository (`.claude/skills/`), which skill takes priority?

agent-skills-41.question: Besides the two basic fields `name` and `description`, what are the two very important optional configuration fields in `SKILL.md` YAML frontmatter covered in Chapter 3?

agent-skills-43.question: According to the 'Writing Effective Descriptions' principle in Chapter 3, what 2 questions should a good `description` always clearly answer?

agent-skills-44.question: What is the exact effect of the `allowed-tools` field in YAML frontmatter (e.g., `allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash`)?

Increases the model's Context Window limit to 10 million tokens

agent-skills-45.question: In the Chapter 3 `codebase-onboarding` skill example with `allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash`, why did the author NOT include `Write` or `Edit` in `allowed-tools`?

agent-skills-46.question: What happens if you completely omit the `allowed-tools` field in `SKILL.md`?

agent-skills-48.question: What problem does the **Progressive Disclosure** principle solve when designing Multi-File Skills?

Automatically deletes Claude's older responses every 30 seconds

agent-skills-52.question: In a Multi-File Skill structure, what is the `assets/` directory best suited to hold?

The company's entire product database
A complete Python interpreter
