`System Prompt` cannot be used.
`Tool Use` cannot be used.
`Response Streaming` cannot be used.
claude-api-121.explanation: Extended Thinking works well with System Prompts, Tool Use, and Streaming, but does NOT allow setting `temperature` to anything other than `1.0` and does NOT allow Assistant Message Prefilling (since Claude must always begin its turn with a `ThinkingBlock`).

claude-api-122.question: What is the purpose of the `signature` field inside each `ThinkingBlock`?
options: It is a cryptographic signature allowing Claude's servers to verify that the `ThinkingBlock` content was genuinely generated by Claude and was not altered or forged by the client when sent back in multi-turn conversation history.
It is the name of the developer who wrote the application.
It is a 90% token cost discount code.
It is a URL link to the Anthropic homepage.
claude-api-122.explanation: To prevent users from tampering with the model's reasoning in chat history, Anthropic attaches a `signature` to each `ThinkingBlock` to verify integrity.

claude-api-123.question: When does `RedactedThinkingBlock` (`type="redacted_thinking"`) appear, and why must we still preserve it in the conversation history for subsequent turns?
options: It appears when part of Claude's internal reasoning triggers safety systems and gets encrypted into the `data` field; we must still pass that `RedactedThinkingBlock` back to Claude on subsequent turns so Claude can decrypt it internally and maintain its reasoning continuity.
It appears when the Internet connection is slow and must be deleted from the `messages` array immediately.
It appears when you forget to pass `max_tokens`.
It only appears when sending PNG image files.
claude-api-123.explanation: When internal safety filters are triggered, Claude encrypts its thinking into `RedactedThinkingBlock(data=...)`. Although the user cannot read the `data` string, passing it back in the chat history lets Claude's server decrypt it to preserve the model's reasoning context.

claude-api-124.question: How can you test whether your application code properly handles `RedactedThinkingBlock` without intentionally asking harmful, policy-violating questions?
options: Send the official test 'Magic String' provided by Anthropic (`ANTHROPIC_MAGIC_STRING_TRIGGER_REDACTED_THINKING_...`) to safely force Claude to return a `RedactedThinkingBlock`.
Turn off the server while calling the API.
Set `budget_tokens = -1`.
Send a corrupted image file.
claude-api-124.explanation: In Lab 28 (`28-extended-thinking`), Anthropic provides a special Magic String specifically for safely triggering and testing `RedactedThinkingBlock` handling.

claude-api-125.question: When sending images (Image Support - Lab 29) to the Claude API, what are the technical limits and the formula for estimating Input Tokens for an image?
options: Maximum **100 images per request**, maximum **5MB per image** (recommended no larger than `1568x1568` px), and approximate tokens equal **`(Width * Height) / 750`**.
Only 1 image under 10KB allowed, always costing a fixed 10 tokens.
Supports images up to 10GB and does not count toward Input Tokens.
Only supports `.bmp` and `.tiff` formats.
claude-api-125.explanation: Claude supports 4 image formats (`image/jpeg`, `image/png`, `image/gif`, `image/webp`), up to 100 images per call, up to 5MB per image, and image token cost is estimated by Tokens ≈ (Width × Height) / 750.

claude-api-126.question: In a User Message containing both an image block (`type="image"`) and a text question block (`type="text"`), what ordering does Anthropic's Best Practice recommend?
options: Place the **Image (`image`) block FIRST**, followed by the **Text question/instruction (`text`) block AFTER**.
Text must be placed first, and the image must be sent in a separate request.
Images and text are not allowed in the same message.
Place the image inside the `stop_sequences` parameter.
claude-api-126.explanation: Placing the image (or PDF document) before the text question allows Claude to observe the full visual data before reading the specific instructions to perform on that image.

claude-api-127.question: When adapting image-reading code (`.png`) to directly read a **PDF** document (`earth.pdf` in Lab 30 `30-pdf-support`), what values should you set for the Content Block's `type` and `media_type` fields?
options: `"type": "document"` and `"media_type": "application/pdf"`
`"type": "pdf"` and `"media_type": "image/pdf"`
`"type": "file"` and `"media_type": "text/pdf"`
`"type": "attachment"` and `"media_type": "binary/octet-stream"`
claude-api-127.explanation: To send a PDF via Base64, use the block `{"type": "document", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": file_bytes}}`.

claude-api-128.question: What can Claude's direct PDF processing capability (PDF Support) read and analyze inside a PDF file?
options: Not only plain text, but also **images, charts, tables, and page layout structure** inside the PDF.
Only unaccented letters, completely ignoring all tables and drawings in the PDF.
Only the first page of the PDF.
Only the PDF filename, not the contents inside.
claude-api-128.explanation: Claude processes each PDF page both as text and visually, allowing it to fully understand charts, illustrations, data tables, and page formatting.

claude-api-129.question: You are building an application where users need to verify the accuracy of information Claude extracts from documents (`verify information Claude provides from documents`). Which feature should you enable and which 2 fields should you add to the `document` block?
options: Enable **`Citations`** by adding `"title": "..."` and `"citations": {"enabled": True}` to the `type="document"` block.
Enable `Code Execution`.
Enable `Prompt Caching`.
Enable `Extended Thinking`.
claude-api-129.explanation: When you include `"title": "earth.pdf"` and `"citations": {"enabled": True}` in the `document` block, Claude automatically attaches a `citations` list to each returned `TextBlock` so users can verify the source.

claude-api-130.question: When enabling `Citations` for a **PDF** document versus a **Plain Text** (`text/plain`) document, how do the location fields in the returned citation objects differ?
options: For **PDF**, Claude returns page numbers (`start_page_number` & `end_page_number`); for **Plain Text** (which has no pages), Claude returns character positions (`start_char_index` & `end_char_index`).
For PDF it returns pixel coordinates, while for Plain Text it returns line numbers.
Both return only the filename without any location.
Plain Text is not allowed to use the Citations feature.
claude-api-130.explanation: Both include `cited_text`, `document_index`, and `document_title`, but PDF uses `start_page_number` / `end_page_number` (`page_location`), whereas Plain Text uses `start_char_index` / `end_char_index` (`char_location`).

claude-api-131.question: You repeatedly send the same long document (or a 6K-token System Prompt + 1.7K-token Tools) to Claude with different questions. How can you make subsequent calls both **faster** and **up to 90% cheaper**?
options: Use **Prompt Caching** by placing Cache Breakpoints (`"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}`).
Compress the document into a `.rar` file before sending.
Split the document into 1000 pieces and send them in 1000 separate requests.
Combine every user's questions into a single question.
claude-api-131.explanation: Prompt Caching stores the processed prefix in a cache on the first call (`Cache Write`, lasting up to 1 hour), allowing subsequent calls (`Cache Read`) to skip recomputing the large document, reducing latency by 80%+ and cache read costs by 90%.

claude-api-132.question: In a single request sent to the Claude API, what is the maximum number of `Cache Breakpoints` (`"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}`) allowed, and what is the minimum token length from the start of the request to the Breakpoint for caching to activate?
options: Up to **4 Cache Breakpoints**, and the content must reach at least **1024 tokens** (if shorter than 1024 tokens, Claude silently skips caching without throwing an error).
Up to 100 Cache Breakpoints and a minimum length of 10 tokens.
Only 1 Cache Breakpoint allowed with no minimum length requirement.
Up to 2 Cache Breakpoints and must be over 50,000 tokens.
claude-api-132.explanation: Anthropic allows up to 4 Cache Breakpoints per request, and the minimum threshold to activate caching is 1024 tokens (or 2048 tokens for some smaller models).

claude-api-133.question: What will a `Cache Breakpoint` attached to Block 2 in a 3-block User Message `[Block 1: PDF, Block 2: Image + cache_control, Block 3: Text Question]` store in the cache?
options: It caches the **entire prefix from the START of the request through the end of Block 2** (meaning BOTH `Block 1: PDF` and `Block 2: Image` are cached, while `Block 3` comes after the breakpoint and is not cached).
It ONLY caches `Block 2: Image` and ignores `Block 1: PDF`.
It only caches `Block 3: Text Question`.
It deletes all of `Block 1` and `Block 2`.
claude-api-133.explanation: Claude's Prompt Caching works on the principle of **Prefix Caching**: wherever `cache_control` is placed, everything from the beginning of the request up to and including that block is packaged into the cache entry.

claude-api-134.question: In what fixed top-to-bottom order does Claude always concatenate the 3 main components of a request, and what happens if you place caches on both `Tools` and `System Prompt` and then modify the `Tools` list?
options: The fixed order is **`1. Tools -> 2. System Prompt -> 3. Messages`**; because `Tools` comes first, modifying `Tools` **INVALIDATES the entire cache for `Tools`, `System Prompt`, and `Messages` that follow it**.
The order is `Messages -> System -> Tools`; modifying `Tools` does not affect `System`.
The three components are cached completely separately so modifying one never affects the others.
Claude does not allow caching `Tools` and `System` at the same time.
claude-api-134.explanation: Because the prefix concatenation order is always `1. Tools -> 2. System -> 3. Messages`, if you keep `Tools` unchanged and only modify `System`, you still get a Partial Cache Read on `Tools`; however, modifying `Tools` at position 1 invalidates every cache layer after it.

claude-api-135.question: In Lab 31 (`31-prompt-caching-in-action`), when attaching `cache_control` to the last tool in the `tools` list, why do we write `tools_clone = tools.copy()` AND `last_tool = tools_clone[-1].copy()` before setting `last_tool["cache_control"] = {"type": "ephemeral"}`?
options: To avoid directly mutating the original tool definition dictionary outside the `chat()` function, in case you reorder the tools on subsequent calls.
Because Python requires calling `.copy()` twice before assigning a key to a dictionary.
To double the number of tools sent to Claude.
To cut the tool's token count in half.
claude-api-135.explanation: If you assign `tools[-1]["cache_control"] = ...` directly, that tool's original dictionary retains the `cache_control` property. If you later reorder the `tools` list, that old tool moving to the middle would still carry `cache_control` and misplace the Breakpoint.

claude-api-136.question: In the `response.usage` object returned when Prompt Caching is enabled, what is the difference between `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens`?
options: `cache_creation_input_tokens` is the number of tokens **newly written to the Cache** (on the first call or when the prefix changes), whereas `cache_read_input_tokens` is the number of tokens **read directly from an existing Cache** (Cache Hit).
`cache_creation_input_tokens` is the number of output tokens in the answer.
Both fields are always 0.
`cache_read_input_tokens` only counts tokens not stored in the Cache.
claude-api-136.explanation: On the first call, you will see `cache_creation_input_tokens > 0` (Cache Write). On subsequent calls with the same prefix within 1 hour, you will see `cache_read_input_tokens > 0` (Cache Read / Hit).

claude-api-137.question: What is the purpose of the `Files API` (`files-api-2025-04-14` in Lab 32)?
options: It allows you to upload large files (PDF, images, CSV, etc.) to Anthropic's servers once (`client.beta.files.upload`) to receive a `file_id`, and then simply reference that `file_id` in subsequent conversations without resending the Base64 string.
It allows Claude to directly access the user's `C:\` drive over the network.
It is used to delete all system files on the server.
It is only used to rename `.txt` files to `.py`.
claude-api-137.explanation: The Files API eliminates having to repeatedly read and Base64-encode the same file over the network on every request; you just upload it once and pass its `file_id`.

claude-api-138.question: What is a key security limitation of Claude's `Code Execution Tool` (`code_execution_20250825`)?
options: It only runs JavaScript.
It has no network access and runs in an isolated Docker container.
It requires users to install Docker on their personal machine.
It only processes plain text `.txt` files.
claude-api-138.explanation: The Code Execution Tool is a server-side tool running on Anthropic's infrastructure inside a completely isolated Docker container with no network access to ensure absolute security.

claude-api-139.question: In Lab 32 (`32-code-execution-and-files-api`), how do you load `streaming.csv` (already uploaded via the Files API with `file_metadata.id`) into the `Code Execution Tool`'s Docker container so Claude can run Python code to analyze it?
options: Attach a `{"type": "container_upload", "file_id": file_metadata.id}` block inside the User Message content and pass `tools=[{"type": "code_execution_20250825", "name": "code_execution"}]`.
Send the path `d:\ai\streaming.csv` as a plain text string.
Put `file_id` inside the `stop_sequences` parameter.
Pass the CSV file through the `temperature` parameter.
claude-api-139.explanation: The `{"type": "container_upload", "file_id": file_metadata.id}` block tells Anthropic's server to copy the file with that `file_id` from the Files API into the Docker container's working directory before running code.

claude-api-140.question: When Claude runs Python data analysis code in the `Code Execution Tool` and generates a new chart image file (e.g., `plt.savefig('churn_plot.png')`), how do you retrieve that chart image onto your local machine?
options: Find the block with `type="bash_code_execution_output"` inside `BashCodeExecutionToolResultBlock` to get the generated image's `file_id`, then call `client.beta.files.download(file_id)`.
Files generated inside the Container cannot be retrieved because the Container is isolated.
Claude will automatically email the file to you.
You must take a screenshot of the Terminal window.
claude-api-140.explanation: Any new file created by Claude's code in the Container is automatically exported to the Files API with a `file_id` in the `bash_code_execution_output` block, allowing you to download it using `download_file(file_id)`.

claude-api-141.question: In the wildfire risk assessment exercise using satellite imagery (Lab 29 `29-image-support`), which prompting technique helps Claude count objects or evaluate image details much more accurately than asking directly for the final conclusion?
options: Ask Claude to identify and list each object's coordinates/features step-by-step before giving the total count or final conclusion (combined with a One-Shot Image Example if available).
Ask Claude to reply with only a single number and no explanation.
Reduce the image resolution to 10x10 pixels.
Rotate the image 180 degrees before sending.
claude-api-141.explanation: Just like text reasoning tasks, in Vision tasks asking Claude to describe and count each region/object in the image before concluding significantly improves visual accuracy.

claude-api-142.question: What critical note was emphasized in Lab 32's prompt when Claude executes multiple consecutive code snippets in the `Code Execution Tool`?
options: Each code execution command may start in a fresh Python process (clean slate), without preserving variables or imported libraries from previous runs, so all required libraries and variables must be re-imported/re-declared.
Each code run is limited to a maximum of 3 lines.
Libraries like `pandas` or `matplotlib` are not allowed.
The CSV file must be deleted after every command.
claude-api-142.explanation: Because each `bash_code_execution` command runs a separate `python3` process in the container, in-memory variables from a previous Python command do not persist to the next, so libraries must be re-imported and data reloaded.

claude-api-143.question: What is the main difference in roles between an `MCP Server` and an `MCP Client`?
options: `MCP Servers` house and provide Tools, Prompts, and Resources, whereas `MCP Clients` act as the communication bridge in your application to access those tools and resources.
`MCP Servers` handle user login, while `MCP Clients` manage permissions.
`MCP Servers` only store static data, while `MCP Clients` execute GitHub API calls.
`MCP Servers` must run in the remote cloud, while `MCP Clients` only run on mobile phones.
claude-api-143.explanation: An MCP Server packages a suite of `Tools`, `Prompts`, and `Resources`, while an MCP Client resides in your application (`Our Server` / IDE) as the bridge connecting to the MCP Server.

claude-api-144.question: What are the 3 Core Primitives that an `MCP Server` can provide to an `MCP Client`?
options: `Tools`, `Resources`, and `Prompts`
`Tables`, `Views`, and `Stored Procedures`
`HTML`, `CSS`, and `JavaScript`
`Models`, `Tokens`, and `Embeddings`
claude-api-144.explanation: Every standard MCP Server exposes up to 3 core primitives: `Tools` (`@mcp.tool`), `Resources` (`@mcp.resource`), and `Prompts` (`@mcp.prompt`).

claude-api-145.question: How does MCP solve `The Tool Function Problem` compared to writing Raw Tool Use yourself?
options: Instead of manually writing, testing, and maintaining dozens of JSON Schema + API call function pairs (like the GitHub API) on your own server, MCP shifts all tool definition and execution work to pre-built `MCP Servers` that you can simply connect to and reuse.
MCP eliminates the need for Claude to ever use Tool Use again.
MCP automatically deletes all function parameters.
MCP replaces the HTTP protocol worldwide.
claude-api-145.explanation: The key difference between MCP and Raw Tool Use comes down to *'Who does the work of writing and maintaining the Tools?'*: with MCP, all Tool Schemas and execution logic are already packaged inside the MCP Server.

claude-api-146.question: What does the concept `'Transport Agnostic'` mean in the MCP protocol?
options: MCP Clients and MCP Servers can communicate over various transport methods such as Standard Input/Output (`stdio`), `HTTP`, or `WebSockets` without changing the underlying protocol message structure.
MCP only works over high-speed fiber-optic connections.
MCP automatically selects the cheapest telecom carrier.
MCP requires dedicated proprietary networking hardware.
claude-api-146.explanation: Transport Agnostic means the MCP protocol separates the logical message layer (JSON-RPC) from the physical transport channel: local processes use `stdio`, while remote connections use `HTTP` / `SSE` / `WebSockets`.

claude-api-147.question: In the 8-step MCP sequence diagram (Section 2C, Chapter 7), which statement is TRUE about the relationship between `Claude` and an `MCP Server`?
options: Claude NEVER connects or talks directly to the `MCP Client` or `MCP Server` — your own application (`Our Server`) acts as the intermediary that fetches the tool list from `MCP Client` to send to `Claude`, and then receives `ToolUseBlock` from `Claude` and hands it to `MCP Client` to call the `MCP Server`.
Claude's servers automatically open a direct connection to `mcp_server.py` on your computer.
`MCP Server` sends results directly to the user's browser without going through `Our Server`.
`MCP Client` resides inside Claude's neural network.
claude-api-147.explanation: This is a crucial architectural point: `Claude` is completely unaware of `MCP Server`. `Our Server` uses `MCP Client` to retrieve schemas to pass into `tools=[...]` for Claude and coordinates `call_tool` execution.

claude-api-148.question: When an `MCP Client` wants to ask an `MCP Server` what tools it has and then execute a tool, which 2 standard message pairs are exchanged?
options: `ListToolsRequest` <-> `ListToolsResult` (to list tools) and `CallToolRequest` <-> `CallToolResult` (to execute a tool)
`GetTools` <-> `PostTools` and `RunCode` <-> `StopCode`
`SelectTools` <-> `UpdateTools`
`Ping` <-> `Pong` and `Login` <-> `Logout`
claude-api-148.explanation: The MCP specification defines `ListToolsRequest` / `ListToolsResult` for `list_tools()` and `CallToolRequest` / `CallToolResult` for `call_tool()`.

claude-api-149.question: When building an `MCP Server` with the Python SDK (`from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP`), what is the greatest benefit of combining the `@mcp.tool(...)` decorator with Python Type Hints and `pydantic.Field(description=...)`?
options: The SDK **automatically generates the entire JSON Schema (`inputSchema`) and validates input types**, freeing developers from writing JSON Schemas manually.
It makes Python code run faster than C.
It automatically generates a 3D GUI for the tool.
You no longer need to write the implementation inside the function body.
claude-api-149.explanation: `FastMCP` inspects Python function signatures, type hints (`: str`, `: float`), and Pydantic's `Field(description=...)` to automatically compile a standard JSON Schema for Claude and validate arguments.

claude-api-150.question: Inside an `@mcp.tool` function on a `FastMCP` Server (such as `read_document`), if `doc_id` does not exist in the `docs` dictionary and you execute `raise ValueError(f"Doc with id {doc_id} not found")`, what happens?
options: `FastMCP` automatically catches this exception and wraps it into a `CallToolResult` response with `isError=True` and a clear error message sent back to the Client/Claude so Claude can understand and handle it.
The entire `mcp_server.py` process crashes and terminates immediately.
`FastMCP` ignores the error and returns the string `"Success"`.
The computer automatically restarts.
claude-api-150.explanation: Raising a Python exception with a clear message (`raise ValueError(...)`) is the standard way in `FastMCP` to report tool errors back to `MCPClient` and `Claude`.

claude-api-151.question: While developing `mcp_server.py`, which command launches the browser-based **MCP Inspector** UI to test and debug Tools, Resources, and Prompts in real time before finishing the `MCP Client`?
options: `mcp dev mcp_server.py` (or `uv run mcp dev mcp_server.py`)
`python --inspect-browser mcp_server.py`
`claude test-mcp mcp_server.py`
`pytest --ui mcp_server.py`
claude-api-151.explanation: The `mcp dev mcp_server.py` command (from the `mcp[cli]` package) starts a local web server (MCP Inspector Dashboard) where you can click Connect and visually test each Tool, Resource, and Prompt in your browser.

claude-api-152.question: In `mcp_client.py` (Lab 33), why do we write a `MCPClient` wrapper class (using `AsyncExitStack`) around the `mcp` SDK's `ClientSession` object?
options: Because `stdio_client` and `ClientSession` open a child process and asynchronous streams that require proper closing and resource cleanup (via `aclose()`) after use.
Because `ClientSession` does not have a `list_tools()` method.
Because `ClientSession` is only written in Java.
To translate the SDK's method names into Vietnamese.
claude-api-152.explanation: Wrapping `stdio_client` and `ClientSession` in `MCPClient` with `AsyncExitStack` and `__aenter__`/`__aexit__` manages the connection lifecycle and ensures safe automatic cleanup when using `async with MCPClient(...) as client:`.

claude-api-153.question: In the MCP protocol, what traditional web architecture concept is `Resources` (`@mcp.resource`) analogous to, and how does it differ from `Tools`?
options: `Resources` are like **`GET` requests** in HTTP/REST APIs — used to expose data for the application/Client to proactively read and display in the UI (such as an `@` autocomplete menu) or inject directly into the prompt's `<context>`.
`Resources` are like `DELETE` requests used to wipe databases.
`Resources` are only called by Claude itself; Client application code can never read them.
`Resources` are only used to run Bash commands inside Docker.
claude-api-153.explanation: Whereas `Tools` are action functions that *Claude* decides to call, `Resources` are data endpoints (like `GET` endpoints) that the *Client application code* proactively calls via `read_resource(uri)` to display in the UI or pre-inject into prompts.

claude-api-154.question: What is the difference between a **Direct / Static Resource** and a **Templated / Parameterized Resource** in `mcp_server.py`?
options: A **Direct Resource** has a fixed URI path (e.g., `"docs://documents"`), whereas a **Templated Resource** contains a dynamic parameter in curly braces in the URI (e.g., `"docs://documents/{doc_id}"`) that automatically maps to the `doc_id` parameter of the Python function.
A Direct Resource always returns images, while a Templated Resource always returns audio.
A Direct Resource does not need the `@mcp.resource` decorator.
A Templated Resource cannot be tested in the MCP Inspector.
claude-api-154.explanation: In the MCP Inspector (Resources tab), Direct Resources (`"docs://documents"`) appear when clicking **List Resources**, while Templated Resources (`"docs://documents/{doc_id}"`) appear when clicking **List Templates**.

claude-api-155.question: When `@mcp.resource("docs://documents", mime_type="application/json") def list_docs() -> list[str]:` returns a Python list of strings `["deposition.md", "report.pdf"]`, what happens on the Server and Client (`read_resource`) sides?
options: On the Server, `FastMCP` automatically serializes the list into a JSON string; on the Client (`read_resource`), seeing `resource.mimeType == "application/json"`, the Client calls `json.loads(resource.text)` to parse it back into a Python list.
The Server throws an error because a Resource is not allowed to return a `list`.
The Client receives the `list` object directly without needing `json.loads()`.
All `.md` and `.pdf` file extensions are stripped from the filenames.
claude-api-155.explanation: The MCP protocol transmits text content as strings in `TextResourceContents`. `FastMCP` automatically converts `list[str]` to a JSON string on the Server, and `mime_type="application/json"` signals `MCPClient.read_resource()` to call `json.loads(resource.text)`.

claude-api-156.question: In `MCPClient.read_resource(self, uri: str)` (Lab 33), why do we wrap the `uri` string in `AnyUrl(uri)` (from `pydantic`) when calling `await self.session().read_resource(AnyUrl(uri))`?
options: Because the MCP SDK's `ClientSession.read_resource()` method requires the URI parameter to be a validated URL object of type `pydantic.AnyUrl`.
To automatically download that webpage from the Internet.
To Base64-encode the URI string.
Because Python does not have a `str` data type.
claude-api-156.explanation: Pydantic's `AnyUrl` ensures the URI string (such as `"docs://documents/report.pdf"`) conforms to the URI syntax expected by `ClientSession.read_resource()`.

claude-api-157.question: What is the biggest performance benefit when the `CliChat` application (Lab 33) automatically detects `@report.pdf` in the user's question, calls `read_resource("docs://documents/report.pdf")`, and embeds its contents directly into the prompt's `<context>` tag before sending to Claude?
options: Claude receives the document contents upfront in the very first message turn and responds immediately, completely eliminating an extra tool-call round trip (`read_doc_contents`).
It makes the model use zero tokens.
It automatically converts `.pdf` files into `.mp4`.
It prevents the user from asking a second question.
claude-api-157.explanation: That is the core advantage of using Resources for Direct Context Injection: it reduces 2 LLM round trips (1 to request the tool + 1 to read the tool result) down to just 1 single call.

claude-api-158.question: You want to provide users with a high-quality, pre-tested instruction for formatting documents. Which MCP feature should you use?
options: `Resources`
`Sessions`
`Tools`
`Prompts` (`@mcp.prompt`)
claude-api-158.explanation: **`Prompts`** (`@mcp.prompt`) in MCP are used to package high-quality, prompt-engineered and pre-tested instruction templates (like the `/format` command) so users and Client apps can invoke them immediately rather than writing prompts from scratch.

claude-api-159.question: What data type does a function decorated with `@mcp.prompt(name="format", ...)` on a `FastMCP` Server return?
options: A list of message objects (`list[base.Message]`, e.g., `return [base.UserMessage(prompt)]` from `mcp.server.fastmcp.prompts import base`)
An integer `int`
A boolean `True` or `False`
A `VectorIndex` object
claude-api-159.explanation: MCP Prompts define a sequence of starter conversation messages (`list[base.Message]`, consisting of `base.UserMessage` or `base.AssistantMessage`) with parameters interpolated for the Client to forward to Claude.

claude-api-160.question: When `MCPClient` calls `await self.session().get_prompt(prompt_name, args)`, what is the mandatory rule for the keys inside the `args` dictionary?
options: The keys in the `args` dictionary (e.g., `{"doc_id": "plan.md"}`) MUST **match the exact parameter names** of the `@mcp.prompt` function defined on the MCP Server (`def format_document(doc_id: str = ...)`).
The keys must always be named `"arg1"`, `"arg2"`, `"arg3"`.
The `args` dictionary must always be empty `{}`.
